chem_edx.8.0.summary: **Hydrocarbons** are compounds that contain **carbon and hydrogen atoms only**. **Crude oil** is a **complex mixture of hydrocarbons** whose molecules contain carbon atoms joined in **chains** or **rings**. Crude oil is an **important source of useful substances**: it provides **fuels** and is the **feedstock for the petrochemical industry**. Because it formed over millions of years and is being used far faster than it can form, crude oil is a **finite resource**.

core.p: A **hydrocarbon** is a compound made of **hydrogen and carbon atoms only**. The word 'only' is essential: if any other element is present, such as oxygen, chlorine or nitrogen, the compound is not a hydrocarbon. Hydrocarbons are compounds, so the carbon and hydrogen atoms are chemically joined by covalent bonds, not just mixed.
bullets: Hydrocarbon = compound of **carbon and hydrogen only**.
Examples: methane CH4, ethane C2H6, propane C3H8, butane C4H10, ethene C2H4, octane C8H18.
Non-examples: ethanol C2H5OH (contains oxygen), carbon dioxide CO2 (contains oxygen, no hydrogen), chloromethane CH3Cl (contains chlorine), glucose C6H12O6 (contains oxygen).
A mixture of carbon and hydrogen gas is NOT a hydrocarbon - a hydrocarbon is a compound.
Hydrocarbons are the main substances found in crude oil and natural gas.

callouts.p: A compound that contains carbon and hydrogen atoms only.
'Contains carbon and hydrogen' without 'only' does not score - ethanol and glucose contain carbon and hydrogen too.

core.p: Hydrocarbon molecules are held together by **covalent bonds** (shared pairs of electrons). Each carbon atom forms **four** covalent bonds and each hydrogen atom forms **one**. This is why carbon can link to other carbon atoms to build long chains and rings, with hydrogen atoms filling the remaining bonding positions.
bullets: Carbon has 4 electrons in its outer shell, so it shares 4 electrons to make 4 bonds.
Hydrogen has 1 outer electron, so it makes 1 bond.
Carbon atoms can bond to each other in long chains, branched chains or rings.
Hydrocarbons are **simple molecular** substances, made of separate molecules.
Small hydrocarbon molecules (e.g. methane) are gases at room temperature; larger ones are liquids or solids.

callouts.p: In a displayed formula of a hydrocarbon, every C has four lines coming off it and every H has exactly one.

core.h: Crude oil is a complex mixture of hydrocarbons
core.p: **Crude oil** is a thick, dark, smelly liquid found in rocks underground. It is not a single substance: it is a **complex mixture** of a very large number of different **hydrocarbons**. 'Complex' means there are many different compounds, with molecules of many different sizes and shapes.
bullets: It is a **mixture**, so the different hydrocarbons are **not chemically joined** to each other.
Each hydrocarbon in the mixture keeps its own properties, such as its own boiling point.
This means the hydrocarbons can be separated by a **physical** method - fractional distillation (see point 8.3-8.5).
The molecules range from very small (1 carbon atom) to very large (over 50 carbon atoms).
Crude oil as it comes out of the ground is not very useful; it must be separated first.

callouts.p: A complex mixture of hydrocarbons, containing molecules in which carbon atoms are in chains or rings.
In a 'describe crude oil' question, score with 'complex mixture' and 'hydrocarbons'.

core.h: Carbon atoms in chains or rings
core.p: The hydrocarbon molecules in crude oil contain carbon atoms joined together in **chains** or in **rings**. Chains can be straight or branched. Rings are closed loops of carbon atoms. You do not need to know the names, formulae or structures of specific ring molecules for Edexcel.
bullets: **Chain** molecules: carbon atoms linked one after another, e.g. propane C3H8 (H3C-CH2-CH3).
Longer chains make bigger molecules, e.g. octane has a chain of 8 carbon atoms.
**Ring** molecules: carbon atoms joined in a closed loop.
Molecules of different sizes and shapes have different boiling points, which helps separate them.
The spec only requires you to know that both chains and rings exist in crude oil.

callouts.p: You will not be asked to name or draw specific ring molecules - do not waste time learning them.

core.h: Crude oil as an important source of useful substances
core.p: Once it has been separated into **fractions**, crude oil provides two main kinds of useful substance: **fuels** and **feedstock for the petrochemical industry**. Modern life depends on both.
bullets: Most crude oil (the large majority) is used to make **fuels**.
A smaller proportion is used as **feedstock** - the raw material for making other chemicals.
Both uses depend on first separating the mixture into fractions with similar boiling points.
Some fractions are also cracked to make smaller, more useful molecules (see point 8.16-8.17).
Because so many products come from crude oil, running out would affect transport, heating, electricity and manufacturing.

core.p: A **fuel** is a substance that releases heat energy when it is burned. Hydrocarbons make excellent fuels because they react with oxygen in very exothermic reactions, releasing large amounts of energy per kilogram.
bullets: **Petrol** - fuel for cars.
**Kerosene** - fuel for aircraft (jet fuel).
**Diesel oil** - fuel for some cars, lorries and trains.
**Fuel oil** - fuel for large ships and some power stations.
**Liquefied petroleum gases (LPG)** - bottled gas for heating and cooking (e.g. camping gas).
**Heating oil** - fuel for heating homes.
When hydrocarbons burn completely they form carbon dioxide and water (combustion is covered in point 8.7-8.10).

callouts.p: If asked for one fuel obtained from crude oil, petrol, diesel oil or kerosene are the safest answers.

core.p: A **feedstock** is a raw material that is used to make other substances in an industrial process. The **petrochemical industry** uses hydrocarbons from crude oil as its feedstock, chemically changing them into a huge range of new materials.
bullets: **Petrochemicals** are substances made from crude oil (via its fractions).
The most important petrochemical products are **polymers (plastics)** such as poly(ethene).
Other products include solvents, detergents and lubricants.
Many feedstock molecules come from **cracking** larger hydrocarbons to make alkenes such as ethene.
Using crude oil as feedstock is a strong reason to conserve it rather than burn it all as fuel.

callouts.p: A raw material used to make other substances in an industrial process.
A substance made from crude oil, used by the petrochemical industry.

core.p: Knowing how crude oil formed explains why it is finite. Crude oil formed from the remains of tiny sea organisms (**plankton**) that lived millions of years ago.
bullets: Tiny plants and animals in ancient seas died and sank to the sea bed.
They were buried under layers of mud and sediment, so there was little oxygen and they did not fully decay.
Over **millions of years**, high **pressure** and **heat** from the layers above slowly changed the remains into crude oil.
Crude oil collects in porous rocks, trapped under non-porous rock, where it can be extracted by drilling.
Because the process takes millions of years, new crude oil cannot be made on a human timescale.

callouts.p: Crude oil takes millions of years to form, but we are using it up in a few hundred years.

core.h: Crude oil is a finite resource
core.p: A **finite resource** is one that is **no longer being made, or is being made extremely slowly**, so there is a limited amount of it. Crude oil is finite because it took millions of years to form and we are using it up much faster than it can be replaced. Eventually, the reserves that can be extracted economically will run out.
bullets: Finite = limited supply; once it is used up it is gone.
Crude oil is being extracted and used far faster than it is formed.
As reserves become harder to reach, extraction becomes more expensive and difficult (e.g. deep-sea drilling).
Finite resources are also described as **non-renewable** (see point 8.15).
Other finite resources include coal, natural gas and metal ores.

callouts.p: A resource that is no longer being made or is being made extremely slowly, so it will eventually run out.
Do not say crude oil 'can never be made again'. It is still forming, but far too slowly (millions of years) to replace what we use.

core.h: Why it matters that crude oil is finite
core.p: Because crude oil will eventually run out, we need to use it carefully and develop alternatives. This links to later points on alternative fuels and non-renewable resources.
bullets: Fuels and feedstock both come from the same limited supply, so burning oil as fuel reduces what is left for making plastics and other petrochemicals.
Ways to conserve crude oil: use less fuel (efficient engines, public transport), recycle plastics, and develop alternative fuels such as hydrogen or biofuels.
As oil becomes scarcer, its price is likely to rise.
Scientists are developing ways to make useful chemicals from other raw materials.

callouts.p: Strong answers link finite supply to BOTH uses: fuels and feedstock for the petrochemical industry.

core.p: Use this list to check that you can state every required fact in the specification's wording.
bullets: Hydrocarbons are compounds that contain **carbon and hydrogen only**.
Crude oil is a **complex mixture of hydrocarbons**.
Crude oil contains molecules in which carbon atoms are in **chains or rings** (names and structures of specific rings not needed).
Crude oil is an **important source of useful substances**: **fuels** and **feedstock for the petrochemical industry**.
Crude oil is a **finite resource**.

callouts.p: Complex mixture of hydrocarbons; chains or rings; source of fuels and feedstock; finite.

analogy.t: Crude oil as a giant bag of mixed LEGO kits
analogy.p: Imagine a huge bag in which the pieces of thousands of different LEGO models have been tipped together. Every piece is either a black brick (carbon) or a small white stud (hydrogen) - nothing else, just like hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen. Some models are long snakes (chains) and some are closed loops (rings), and they come in all sizes: a complex mixture. You can sort the models by size and either burn them for warmth (fuels) or rebuild them into new toys (feedstock). The bag was filled over millions of years and no one is topping it up fast enough, so once it is empty it is gone - a finite resource. Where it breaks down: LEGO models are just pushed together, while hydrocarbon atoms are joined by covalent bonds; and real hydrocarbons are separated by boiling point, not by looking at them.

exam.q: Which of these is a hydrocarbon: C2H5OH, C3H8, CO2, CH3Cl? Give a reason.

It contains only carbon and hydrogen (the others contain oxygen or chlorine)

of hydrocarbons

It releases (heat) energy when it burns / combusts

exam.q: Crude oil is used both as a source of fuels and as a feedstock for the petrochemical industry. Discuss the importance of crude oil and why it should be conserved.
model: Crude oil is a complex mixture of hydrocarbons, with carbon atoms in chains or rings
It is separated into fractions that are useful
Fractions provide fuels such as petrol, diesel and kerosene for transport and heating
Fractions are feedstock for the petrochemical industry to make polymers/plastics, solvents, detergents
Crude oil is finite: it formed over millions of years and is no longer being made / is made extremely slowly, so it will run out

worked.q: Classify each substance as a hydrocarbon or not: methane CH4, ethene C2H4, ethanoic acid CH3COOH, hexane C6H14, tetrachloromethane CCl4.
steps: Rule: a hydrocarbon contains carbon and hydrogen atoms only.
CH4: only C and H, so hydrocarbon.
C2H4: only C and H, so hydrocarbon.
CH3COOH: contains O, so not a hydrocarbon.
C6H14: only C and H, so hydrocarbon.
CCl4: contains Cl and no H, so not a hydrocarbon.
worked.ans: Hydrocarbons: CH4, C2H4, C6H14. Not hydrocarbons: CH3COOH, CCl4.

worked.q: Write a model answer (4 marks): Describe crude oil and explain why it is a finite resource.
steps: Crude oil is a complex mixture of hydrocarbons (compounds of carbon and hydrogen only).
The molecules contain carbon atoms arranged in chains or rings.
Crude oil formed from the remains of plankton over millions of years, so it is no longer being made or is being made extremely slowly.
We are using it much faster than it forms, so supplies are limited and will eventually run out - it is finite.
worked.ans: A complex mixture of hydrocarbons with chains or rings of carbon atoms; finite because it forms extremely slowly and is being used up faster than it can be replaced.

worked.q: A student says: 'Plastics don't use up crude oil because we don't burn them.' Explain why this is wrong.
steps: Plastics (polymers) are made by the petrochemical industry.
The petrochemical industry uses hydrocarbons from crude oil as its feedstock (raw material).
So every plastic item uses some of the finite supply of crude oil.
Recycling plastics reduces the amount of new crude oil needed as feedstock.
worked.ans: Plastics are made from crude oil used as feedstock, so making them does use up the finite crude oil supply even though they are not burned.

chem_edx.8.1.summary: Crude oil is a complex mixture of hydrocarbons, mostly alkanes, that is not useful until it is separated. **Fractional distillation** heats crude oil until it vaporises, then lets the vapours rise up a **fractionating column** that is hot at the bottom and cool at the top, so each fraction condenses at a different height according to its boiling point range. The main fractions are **gases, petrol, kerosene, diesel oil, fuel oil and bitumen**, each with its own uses. As molecules get longer down the column, they contain more carbon and hydrogen atoms, have higher boiling points, are harder to ignite and are more viscous.

core.h: What crude oil is and why it must be separated
core.p: Crude oil is a thick, dark liquid found in rocks. It is a **complex mixture of hydrocarbons**, compounds containing **hydrogen and carbon atoms only**. Most of these hydrocarbons are **alkanes**, with carbon atoms joined in chains (and some rings). Because it is a mixture, its components are **not chemically bonded to each other**, so they can be separated by a physical method. Crude oil itself is of little use; the separated fractions are far more useful.
bullets: A **hydrocarbon** contains hydrogen and carbon atoms **only** (not 'hydrogen, carbon and oxygen').
Crude oil contains molecules with chains from 1 carbon atom up to more than 50 carbon atoms.
The different hydrocarbons have **different boiling points**, which is the property used to separate them.
Fractional distillation separates crude oil into **simpler, more useful mixtures** called fractions.
It is a **physical** process: no chemical bonds inside the molecules are broken (unlike cracking).
Most hydrocarbons in crude oil belong to the **alkane homologous series**, general formula CnH2n+2.

callouts.p: A **mixture of hydrocarbons** with a **similar number of carbon atoms** and **similar boiling points** (a narrow boiling point range) that condenses at the same level in the fractionating column.

callouts.t: A fraction is not a pure substance
callouts.p: Each fraction is still a mixture, just a **simpler** one. Do not say fractional distillation produces 'pure compounds'.

core.h: Step 1: Heating and vaporising the crude oil
core.p: The crude oil is heated in a furnace to about 350 °C. At this temperature most of the hydrocarbons **evaporate (vaporise)** to form a hot mixture of vapours. The very largest molecules, which have the highest boiling points, stay as a hot liquid.
bullets: Crude oil is **heated strongly** so that it **evaporates / vaporises**.
The hot vapours are fed into the **bottom of the fractionating column**.
Very long-chain hydrocarbons do not vaporise; they form the residue (bitumen) that is drained from the bottom.
Heating supplies the energy needed to overcome the **intermolecular forces** between molecules so they can separate into a gas.

callouts.p: Say **evaporates / boils / vaporises** for heating and **condenses** for cooling. 'Melts' and 'solidifies' lose the mark.

core.h: Step 2: The temperature gradient in the column
core.p: The fractionating column is **hot at the bottom and cooler at the top**. This **temperature gradient** is the key to separation. As vapours rise, they cool down. Each hydrocarbon condenses when the temperature falls below its boiling point.
bullets: Bottom of the column: about 350 °C (hottest).
Top of the column: about 25 °C (coolest).
The column contains horizontal **trays** with holes (bubble caps) that let vapour pass upwards and collect condensed liquid.
Vapours **rise** up the column and **cool** as they go up.
A hydrocarbon **condenses** at the level where the temperature is just **below its boiling point**.
The condensed liquid is collected on the tray and **piped off** (tapped off) at that level.

callouts.p: Different hydrocarbons have **different boiling points**, so they **condense at different heights** in a column that has a **temperature gradient** (hot at the bottom, cool at the top).

Each fraction condenses where the temperature falls below its boiling point and is piped off. Gases leave at the top and bitumen is drained from the bottom.

core.h: Step 3: Condensing and collecting the fractions
core.p: Hydrocarbons with **high boiling points** (long chains) condense **near the bottom**, where it is still hot. Hydrocarbons with **low boiling points** (short chains) stay as vapour until they reach the cool **top** of the column. The smallest molecules never condense in the column and leave at the top as **gases**.
bullets: **Long-chain** molecules: high boiling point, condense **low down**, collected near the **bottom**.
**Short-chain** molecules: low boiling point, rise **higher**, collected near the **top**.
Gases (methane, ethane, propane, butane) have boiling points below the temperature at the top, so they leave the top **as gases**.
**Bitumen** does not vaporise and is removed from the very bottom as a thick residue.
The process is **continuous**: crude oil is fed in and fractions are drawn off all the time.

callouts.p: Heat crude oil, it vaporises -> vapour enters column -> column hot at bottom, cool at top -> vapours rise and cool -> each hydrocarbon condenses when it reaches a level below its boiling point -> fractions with similar boiling points collected at same level -> long chains/high bp at bottom, short chains/low bp at top, gases out of the top.

core.h: The six fractions you must name
core.p: Edexcel names six fractions. Learn them **in order from top to bottom**: **gases, petrol, kerosene, diesel oil, fuel oil, bitumen**. A useful memory aid: 'Good People Keep Doing Fun Business'.
bullets: **Gases** (refinery gases) leave the top of the column.
**Petrol** (gasoline) is collected near the top.
**Kerosene** (paraffin) comes next.
**Diesel oil** (gas oil) is in the middle.
**Fuel oil** is collected lower down.
**Bitumen** is the residue at the very bottom.

callouts.p: Carbon numbers and temperatures vary between textbooks. Exam questions give you data if they need exact values; what matters is the **order** and the **trend**.

core.p: Edexcel requires you to know that the fractions are used **as fuels** (except bitumen) and to recall a specific use for each. Uses match the properties: small molecules that ignite easily and flow easily make good fuels for engines, whereas the thick, sticky residue is good for sealing surfaces.
bullets: **Gases**: used in **domestic heating and cooking** (bottled gas such as propane and butane).
**Petrol**: used as **fuel for cars**.
**Kerosene**: used as **fuel for aircraft** (jet fuel).
**Diesel oil**: used as **fuel for some cars and trains** (and lorries).
**Fuel oil**: used as **fuel for large ships** and in **some power stations**.
**Bitumen**: used to **surface roads and roofs** (it is sticky, waterproof and solid when cool).
Some fractions are also used as **feedstock** for the petrochemical industry to make polymers, solvents and other chemicals.

callouts.p: gases = heating and cooking; petrol = cars; kerosene = aircraft; diesel oil = cars and trains; fuel oil = large ships and power stations; bitumen = roads and roofs.

core.h: Trend 1: number of carbon and hydrogen atoms
core.p: Going **down** the column, the hydrocarbon molecules in each fraction contain **more carbon atoms and more hydrogen atoms**, so they are **longer chains** with a **larger molecular size**. For alkanes the number of hydrogen atoms is always 2n + 2, so more carbon automatically means more hydrogen.
bullets: Gases: about C1 to C4, e.g. CH4, C3H8.
Petrol: e.g. octane C8H18.
Diesel: e.g. hexadecane C16H34.
Bitumen: more than 50 carbon atoms per molecule.
Bigger molecules have a **larger mass** and a **larger surface area** for intermolecular forces.

callouts.p: Edexcel's wording is 'number of **carbon and hydrogen** atoms their molecules contain'. Mention both.

core.p: Fractions lower in the column have **higher boiling points**. This is because longer molecules have **stronger intermolecular forces** between them, so **more energy** is needed to separate the molecules and turn the liquid into a gas.
bullets: Short chains: weak intermolecular forces, low boiling point, collected at the top.
Long chains: stronger intermolecular forces, high boiling point, collected at the bottom.
Boiling a hydrocarbon overcomes the forces **between** molecules; the **covalent bonds inside** the molecules are **not broken**.
Larger molecules have more points of contact with neighbours, so the total attraction is greater.

callouts.p: Never write 'bonds break when crude oil boils'. Say **intermolecular forces** are overcome. Breaking covalent bonds happens in **cracking**, not distillation.

core.p: Fractions higher in the column **ignite more easily** (they are more flammable). Short-chain hydrocarbons are **more volatile**: they evaporate easily, so a flammable vapour forms readily above the liquid and catches fire quickly. Long-chain hydrocarbons are hard to ignite.
bullets: Gases and petrol: **very easy to ignite**, burn with a clean flame.
Diesel and fuel oil: **harder to ignite**.
Bitumen: **very hard to ignite**.
This is why petrol is dangerous to handle near flames, but bitumen can be heated to spread on roads.
Ease of ignition links to the use of short-chain fractions as **fuels for engines**.

callouts.p: As chain length **increases**, ease of ignition **decreases**. Write the trend in a full comparative sentence.

core.p: **Viscosity** is how thick a liquid is, or how **resistant it is to flowing**. Fractions lower down the column are **more viscous**. Longer molecules have stronger intermolecular forces and can **tangle** with each other, so they cannot slide past one another easily.
bullets: Petrol: **runny**, low viscosity, flows easily.
Diesel and fuel oil: **thicker**, more viscous.
Bitumen: **very viscous**, almost solid at room temperature.
More viscous = flows **more slowly**.
Viscosity increases as the number of carbon atoms increases.

callouts.p: A measure of how **easily a liquid flows**. A **viscous** liquid is thick and flows **slowly**.

core.p: All four trends come from one cause: **molecule size**. As you go **down** the column, molecules get bigger, so intermolecular forces get stronger. That raises the boiling point and viscosity and makes the fraction harder to ignite.
bullets: Down the column: **more C and H atoms**, **higher boiling point**, **harder to ignite**, **more viscous**.
Up the column: **fewer C and H atoms**, **lower boiling point**, **easier to ignite**, **less viscous (runnier)**.
Colour also darkens down the column (pale/colourless at top, black at bottom), though Edexcel does not require this.

core.p: Most of the hydrocarbons in each fraction are **alkanes**, members of the same **homologous series** with general formula **CnH2n+2**. Alkanes are **saturated**: they contain only **single C-C bonds**. Because members of a homologous series show a gradual trend in physical properties as chain length increases, the fractions show the smooth trends described above.
bullets: Alkanes: methane CH4, ethane C2H6, propane C3H8, butane C4H10.
Each successive alkane differs by **CH2**.
Gradual increase in boiling point with chain length is a **homologous series** property.
Alkanes are useful fuels because they release a lot of energy when they burn.

callouts.p: Fractions are mostly alkanes, so their trends in boiling point and viscosity follow the trends of the alkane homologous series.

core.p: Fractional distillation gives fixed amounts of each fraction, but these amounts do not match what people want. There is usually **too much** of the long-chain fractions and **not enough** short-chain fractions such as petrol. This mismatch is why the refinery also uses **cracking** (covered in 8.16-8.17).
bullets: Long-chain fractions: high supply, lower demand.
Short-chain fractions (petrol, gases): high demand.
Fractional distillation separates; it does not change molecule size.
Crude oil is a **finite resource**, so fractions should be used efficiently.

callouts.p: Fractional distillation is a **physical separation** based on boiling point. Cracking is a **chemical reaction** that breaks long molecules into shorter ones.

analogy.t: A multi-storey car park with height bars
analogy.p: Imagine a stream of people climbing the stairs of a tall, chilly building, where it gets colder on every floor. Each person carries a heavy rucksack: the bigger the rucksack (the longer the molecule), the sooner they get tired and sit down. People with huge rucksacks (bitumen, fuel oil) stop on the bottom floors; people with tiny bags (petrol, gases) reach the top or walk straight out of the roof. Everyone who stops on the same floor forms a 'fraction'. Where it breaks down: molecules do not get 'tired'. They stop rising because they **condense** when the temperature falls below their boiling point, and that boiling point depends on the strength of **intermolecular forces**, not effort. Also, people on one floor are not all identical: a fraction is still a mixture of similar molecules.

terms.d: A complex mixture of hydrocarbons, mostly alkanes, formed over millions of years from the remains of ancient sea organisms; a finite resource.
A compound containing hydrogen and carbon atoms only.
A physical process that separates a mixture of liquids with different boiling points, using a fractionating column with a temperature gradient.
A simpler mixture of hydrocarbons with similar numbers of carbon atoms and similar boiling points, collected at the same level in the column.
A tall tower that is hot at the bottom and cool at the top, in which crude oil vapour separates into fractions.
A steady change in temperature with height; in the column it falls from about 350 °C at the bottom to about 25 °C at the top.
Change from liquid to gas; crude oil is heated so that it evaporates before entering the column.
Change from gas to liquid when cooled below the boiling point.
The temperature at which a liquid turns into a gas throughout; higher for longer hydrocarbon chains.
Weak forces of attraction between molecules; stronger between larger molecules, so these have higher boiling points.
How resistant a liquid is to flowing; viscous liquids are thick and flow slowly.
How easily a substance catches fire; decreases as chain length increases.
Evaporates easily at low temperature; short-chain hydrocarbons are volatile.
A saturated hydrocarbon with only single C-C bonds and general formula CnH2n+2.
The thick, very viscous residue from the bottom of the column, used to surface roads and roofs.
Fraction used as fuel for aircraft.

mistakes.w: Crude oil is a compound of hydrogen and carbon.
mistakes.r: Crude oil is a **mixture** of hydrocarbons (compounds of hydrogen and carbon only).

mistakes.w: The column is hot at the top and cold at the bottom.
mistakes.r: The column is **hot at the bottom and cool at the top**.

mistakes.w: Covalent bonds break when the crude oil is boiled.
mistakes.r: **Intermolecular forces** between molecules are overcome; covalent bonds within molecules do not break.

mistakes.w: Long-chain molecules rise to the top because they are heavier... / short chains collect at the bottom.
mistakes.r: Long chains have high boiling points and condense **near the bottom**; short chains rise to the **top**.

mistakes.w: Each fraction is a pure substance.
mistakes.r: Each fraction is a **simpler mixture** of hydrocarbons with similar boiling points.

mistakes.w: Longer hydrocarbons are more flammable / ignite more easily.
mistakes.r: Longer hydrocarbons are **harder** to ignite; short chains ignite more easily.

mistakes.w: Viscosity means how fast it boils / how thick it is when solid.
mistakes.r: Viscosity is how **easily a liquid flows**; longer chains are **more viscous**.

mistakes.w: Kerosene is used in cars; diesel is used in aircraft.
mistakes.r: Kerosene = **aircraft** fuel; diesel oil = fuel for **some cars and trains**; petrol = **cars**.

mistakes.w: Fractions are separated by melting point / by density.
mistakes.r: They are separated by **boiling point**: each condenses at a different height.

exam.q: State what is meant by a hydrocarbon.
model: A compound containing hydrogen and carbon (atoms) only.
exam.tip: 'Only' is the mark. 'Contains hydrogen and carbon' alone does not score.

exam.q: Name the fraction obtained from crude oil that is used as fuel for aircraft.
model: Kerosene.
exam.tip: Learn the six fraction-use pairs exactly as the spec lists them.

exam.q: Give one use of bitumen.
model: Surfacing roads / roofs.
exam.tip: 'Making roads' is accepted; 'fuel' is not.

exam.q: Crude oil is separated by fractional distillation. State the physical property of hydrocarbons that allows them to be separated in this way.
model: (Different) boiling points.
exam.tip: Not 'melting point', 'density' or 'size' alone.

exam.q: Fuel oil is collected lower in the fractionating column than petrol. Compare the molecules in fuel oil with those in petrol in terms of number of carbon atoms and boiling point.
model: Fuel oil molecules contain more carbon (and hydrogen) atoms / have longer chains.
Fuel oil has a higher boiling point.
exam.tip: Comparison questions need comparative words: more, higher, longer.

exam.q: Explain why diesel oil is more viscous than petrol.
model: Diesel molecules are larger / have longer chains / more carbon atoms.
So there are stronger (intermolecular) forces between the molecules, so they do not flow past each other as easily.
exam.tip: Link the property to molecule size and forces between molecules.

exam.q: Explain why the gases fraction leaves from the top of the fractionating column.
model: The gases have very low boiling points / small molecules.
They do not condense because the temperature at the top of the column is above their boiling points.
exam.tip: Mention both the low boiling point and the temperature at the top.

exam.q: State the order of fractions from the top of the column to the bottom.
model: gases, petrol, kerosene, diesel oil, fuel oil, bitumen (all correct = 2 marks).
Any four in the correct relative order = 1 mark.
exam.tip: Mnemonic: Good People Keep Doing Fun Business.

exam.q: Describe how the ease of ignition and viscosity change from petrol to bitumen.
model: Ease of ignition decreases / bitumen is harder to ignite.
Viscosity increases / bitumen is more viscous (thicker).
exam.tip: Give the direction of each trend clearly in its own sentence.

exam.q: Describe and explain how crude oil is separated into fractions by fractional distillation.
model: Crude oil is heated so that it evaporates / vaporises.
The vapour enters (the bottom of) a fractionating column.
The column has a temperature gradient: hot at the bottom, cool at the top.
Vapours rise up the column and cool.
Each hydrocarbon condenses when it reaches a level where the temperature is below its boiling point.
Hydrocarbons with similar boiling points / similar numbers of carbon atoms condense at the same level and are collected as a fraction.
Long-chain / high boiling point fractions (e.g. bitumen, fuel oil) are collected at the bottom; short-chain / low boiling point fractions (e.g. petrol) near the top.
Gases leave from the top without condensing.
exam.tip: Write it as a sequence. A 6-mark answer at top level needs the process in logical order AND the explanation using boiling points.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of the forces between molecules, why bitumen has a higher boiling point than kerosene.
model: Bitumen molecules are larger / have more carbon atoms / longer chains.
So the intermolecular forces between bitumen molecules are stronger.
More energy is needed to overcome these forces (so the boiling point is higher).
exam.tip: Avoid saying 'bonds break'. Covalent bonds within the molecule stay intact.

worked.q: A hydrocarbon from crude oil has the formula C12H26. It boils at 216 °C. Use the table of fractions to suggest which fraction it is in, and predict how its viscosity and ease of ignition compare with petrol.
steps: Count the carbon atoms: 12.
Check it is an alkane: CnH2n+2 with n = 12 gives C12H26, so yes.
12 carbon atoms and a boiling point of about 216 °C fall in the kerosene range (about C10 to C16, about 150 to 250 °C).
Kerosene is below petrol in the column, so its molecules are longer than petrol molecules.
Longer molecules mean stronger intermolecular forces: more viscous and harder to ignite.
worked.ans: Kerosene; it is more viscous and harder to ignite than petrol.

worked.q: Data: hydrocarbon A boils at 69 °C, B at 287 °C, C at 36 °C. The column top is 25 °C. Put them in order of the height at which they condense (highest first) and explain which has the longest chain.
steps: Lower boiling point = condenses higher up (cooler region).
Order of boiling points: C (36 °C) < A (69 °C) < B (287 °C).
So condensing height, highest first: C, then A, then B.
All are above 25 °C, so all condense inside the column.
B has the highest boiling point, so it has the strongest intermolecular forces and therefore the longest chain.
worked.ans: C highest, then A, then B. B has the longest chain.

worked.q: Model answer: Suggest why petrol is a better fuel for a car engine than fuel oil.
steps: Petrol molecules are short chains (about C5 to C10).
They are volatile and ignite easily, so the fuel catches fire readily in the engine.
Petrol has low viscosity, so it flows easily through fuel pipes and injectors.
Fuel oil molecules are much longer, are hard to ignite and are viscous, so they would not burn readily or flow easily in a small engine.
worked.ans: Petrol ignites easily and flows easily (low viscosity) because its molecules are short; fuel oil is hard to ignite and viscous.

chem_edx.8.2.summary: A **homologous series** is a family of compounds that have the **same general formula**, where each member **differs from the next by CH2**, that show a **gradual variation in physical properties** such as boiling point, and that have **similar chemical properties**. The alkanes, CnH2n+2, are the main example in Topic 8, and most of the hydrocarbons in crude oil belong to this series. Understanding the series lets you predict the formula, boiling point and reactions of a member you have never met.

core.p: Edexcel defines a homologous series by **four features**. Mark schemes reward each one separately, so learn all four as a list. Think of a homologous series as a chemical 'family': the members look alike, behave alike, and grow in a regular pattern.
bullets: **Same general formula** (for alkanes, CnH2n+2).
**Differ by CH2** in their molecular formulae from neighbouring compounds.
Show a **gradual variation in physical properties**, as shown by their **boiling points**.
Have **similar chemical properties** (they react in the same way).
Members also have the **same functional group** where there is one (e.g. C=C in alkenes), which is why their chemistry is similar.

callouts.p: A series of compounds which have the **same general formula**, **differ by CH2** in molecular formulae from neighbouring compounds, show a **gradual variation in physical properties** (for example boiling points) and have **similar chemical properties**.
A 3 or 4 mark 'describe the features' question is usually one mark per feature. Use the exact phrases 'same general formula', 'differ by CH2', 'gradual variation' and 'similar chemical properties'.

core.p: A **general formula** is an algebraic formula that gives the molecular formula of **any** member of the series when you substitute the number of carbon atoms, n. For the alkanes it is **CnH2n+2**: double the number of carbons and add two to get the number of hydrogens.
bullets: Alkanes: **CnH2n+2**. n = 1 gives CH4; n = 5 gives C5H12; n = 10 gives C10H22.
Alkenes (another homologous series): **CnH2n**, e.g. C2H4, C3H6.
You can use the general formula to **predict** the formula of any member.
You can also use it to **check** whether a formula belongs to a series: C7H16 fits CnH2n+2 (2 x 7 + 2 = 16), so it is an alkane.
C6H12 does **not** fit CnH2n+2, so it is not an alkane.

callouts.p: A formula that shows the ratio of atoms in **all members** of a homologous series, written in terms of n, e.g. CnH2n+2.

core.p: Each member of the series has **one more carbon atom and two more hydrogen atoms** than the member before it. So the molecular formulae of neighbouring compounds differ by **CH2**. In structural terms, an extra **-CH2-** unit is inserted into the chain.
bullets: CH4 -> C2H6 -> C3H8 -> C4H10: each step adds **CH2**.
The relative formula mass increases by **14** each time (C = 12, H = 1, so 12 + 2 = 14).
The chain gets **longer by one carbon** each step.
Note: the difference is CH2, **not** 'CH' or 'C2H4'.

callouts.p: Saying neighbours 'differ by one carbon' is incomplete. They differ by **CH2**: one carbon AND two hydrogens.

core.h: The first members of the alkanes
core.p: You should be able to name and give the formula of the first few alkanes. The names all end in **-ane**, and the start of the name tells you the number of carbons: **meth = 1, eth = 2, prop = 3, but = 4**, then pent, hex and so on.
bullets: Memory aid for the prefixes: **Monkeys Eat Peanut Butter** (meth, eth, prop, but).
All alkanes are **saturated**: only **single** C-C and C-H covalent bonds.
Every carbon atom makes **4 bonds**; every hydrogen atom makes **1 bond**.
Alkanes are **hydrocarbons**: hydrogen and carbon atoms only.

core.h: Feature 3: gradual variation in physical properties
core.p: As the chain gets longer, physical properties change **gradually and predictably**, not suddenly. Edexcel uses **boiling point** as the example: boiling point **increases** steadily as the number of carbon atoms increases. Other physical properties, such as viscosity and state at room temperature, also change gradually.
bullets: Boiling point **increases** as n increases.
Small alkanes (C1 to C4) are **gases** at room temperature; from C5 they are **liquids**; very long ones are **solids** (waxes).
Viscosity **increases** and ease of ignition **decreases** with chain length.
This gradual change is what makes fractional distillation of crude oil possible: fractions of different chain lengths have different boiling points.
The increase is smooth, so you can **estimate** a missing boiling point from a graph or table.

callouts.p: Physical properties (boiling point, viscosity, state) **change gradually** across the series. Chemical properties (how they react) **stay similar**.

core.p: Boiling a simple molecular substance such as an alkane means overcoming the **weak intermolecular forces** between its molecules. Longer molecules are **larger** with **more surface contact** between neighbouring molecules, so the intermolecular forces are **stronger**. More energy is needed to overcome them, so the boiling point is higher.
bullets: Longer chain -> larger molecule -> **stronger intermolecular forces**.
Stronger forces -> **more energy** needed to separate molecules -> **higher boiling point**.
The **covalent bonds within** the molecule are **not broken** on boiling.
Each extra CH2 adds roughly the same extra attraction, which is why the rise is gradual.

callouts.p: Writing 'more bonds to break' scores zero. Boiling overcomes **intermolecular forces**, not covalent bonds.

core.p: Members of a homologous series **react in the same way** because they have the **same type of bonding** and the same functional group (if any). For example, all alkanes undergo **combustion** in plenty of oxygen to give **carbon dioxide and water**. Their reactions differ only slightly in rate or vigour.
bullets: All alkanes burn in oxygen: complete combustion gives **carbon dioxide + water**.
Alkanes are fairly **unreactive** apart from burning, because C-C and C-H single bonds are strong.
All alkenes react with **bromine water**, decolourising it, because they all contain **C=C**.
So if you know the chemistry of one member, you can **predict** the chemistry of the others.
Balanced equations follow the same pattern, just with different numbers.

callouts.p: If asked to 'explain what is meant by similar chemical properties', give a reaction: 'all alkanes burn to form carbon dioxide and water'.

core.p: Homologous series are not only alkanes. **Alkenes** are a second series of hydrocarbons, with general formula **CnH2n** and a **C=C double bond** as their functional group. They show the same four features. Recognising a second series helps you show you understand the idea rather than just the alkanes.
bullets: Alkenes: ethene C2H4, propene C3H6, butene C4H8.
They also differ by **CH2** from one member to the next.
They are **unsaturated** (contain a C=C double bond).
Other series you will meet in triple chemistry: alcohols and carboxylic acids.
There is **no** methene: the smallest alkene must have two carbons to form C=C.

core.h: Using the general formula in calculations
core.p: Exam questions often ask you to work out a formula, a relative formula mass or a number of hydrogen atoms. Always substitute into the general formula carefully, then check by counting.
bullets: Number of H atoms in an alkane = **2n + 2**.
Number of C atoms from H: n = (H - 2) / 2.
Mr of an alkane = 12n + (2n + 2) = **14n + 2**.
Example: an alkane with Mr = 100: 14n + 2 = 100, so n = 7, formula C7H16 (heptane).
Example: an alkane with 30 hydrogen atoms: n = (30 - 2)/2 = 14, so C14H30.

callouts.p: After finding a formula, plug it back into CnH2n+2. If the H count is odd or does not match, you have made an error.

core.p: Because physical properties vary gradually, you can **predict** values for members not shown in a table. Look at the pattern (the difference between successive values) and extend it, or read it from a graph. The increase in boiling point gets slightly smaller as the chains get longer, so the graph curves gently.
bullets: Heptane (C7H16) would have a boiling point **higher than hexane (69 °C)**, about 98 °C.
Its state at room temperature: **liquid**.
It would burn to form **carbon dioxide and water**, like the other alkanes.
Always say **'higher than'** or **'between X and Y'** if you are not given a graph to read accurately.

callouts.p: Physical property: predict by extending the **trend**. Chemical property: predict it is the **same** as other members.

core.h: Link to crude oil and fuels
core.p: Most of the hydrocarbons in crude oil are **alkanes**, so the fractions obtained by fractional distillation show the gradual trends of the alkane homologous series. Short alkanes in the gases and petrol fractions have low boiling points; long alkanes in fuel oil and bitumen have high boiling points.
bullets: Fractions differ in **number of carbon atoms**, so they differ in **boiling point**.
All the alkane fractions burn as **fuels**, an example of similar chemical properties.
Cracking turns long alkanes into shorter alkanes **and alkenes**, so products belong to two different homologous series.

analogy.p: A homologous series is like a staircase built from identical bricks. Every step is made the same way (same general formula and same chemistry), each step is exactly one brick higher than the last (differ by CH2), and the height rises steadily as you climb (gradual increase in boiling point). If you know the size of a brick, you can predict the height of step 10 without seeing it. Where it breaks down: a real staircase rises by exactly the same height each step, but boiling points rise by slightly smaller amounts as chains get longer. Also, the 'bricks' (CH2 units) are joined by covalent bonds, and the property that rises is caused by intermolecular forces between separate molecules, not by stacking.

terms.d: A series of compounds with the same general formula, differing by CH2 from neighbours, showing gradual variation in physical properties and similar chemical properties.
An algebraic formula, in terms of n, that gives the molecular formula of any member of a homologous series.
The actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule, e.g. C3H8.
A diagram showing every atom and every covalent bond in a molecule as a line.
A compound containing hydrogen and carbon atoms only.
A saturated hydrocarbon with only single bonds and general formula CnH2n+2.
An unsaturated hydrocarbon containing a C=C double bond, general formula CnH2n.
Containing only single carbon-carbon bonds.
Containing at least one carbon-carbon double bond.
An atom or group of atoms that gives a homologous series its characteristic chemical reactions, e.g. C=C.
A property that can be observed without a chemical change, e.g. boiling point, viscosity, state.
How a substance reacts, e.g. burning in oxygen.
The temperature at which a liquid changes to a gas; increases with chain length in a homologous series.
Weak attractions between molecules that are overcome when a simple molecular substance boils.
The sum of the relative atomic masses of all atoms in the formula; increases by 14 for each extra CH2.

mistakes.w: Members of a homologous series have the same molecular formula.
mistakes.r: They have the same **general** formula; their molecular formulae are different.

mistakes.w: Neighbouring members differ by one carbon atom / by CH.
mistakes.r: They differ by **CH2**.

mistakes.w: Members have the same physical properties.
mistakes.r: Physical properties show a **gradual variation** (e.g. boiling point increases).

mistakes.w: Members have different chemical properties.
mistakes.r: Members have **similar** chemical properties (react in the same way).

mistakes.w: Boiling point increases because there are more covalent bonds to break.
mistakes.r: Longer molecules have **stronger intermolecular forces**, needing more energy to overcome.

mistakes.w: The general formula of alkanes is CnH2n.
mistakes.r: Alkanes are **CnH2n+2**; CnH2n is the alkenes.

mistakes.w: C4H10 is called propane.
mistakes.r: C4H10 is **butane**; propane is C3H8.

mistakes.w: Methene is the first alkene.
mistakes.r: The first alkene is **ethene, C2H4**; an alkene needs at least two carbons.

exam.q: State the general formula of the alkanes.
model: CnH2n+2
exam.tip: Write the 2n+2 clearly; CnH2n is the alkenes.

exam.q: Give the molecular formula of the alkane with 8 carbon atoms.
model: C8H18

exam.q: Methane, ethane and propane are members of the same homologous series. State the difference in molecular formula between neighbouring members.
model: CH2
exam.tip: Write the formula, not 'one carbon'.

exam.q: State two features, other than having the same general formula, of compounds in a homologous series.
model: Neighbouring members differ by CH2.
Gradual variation in physical properties / boiling points (accept: similar chemical properties).
exam.tip: Any two of the remaining three features; avoid repeating the one in the question.

exam.q: Describe what is meant by a homologous series.
model: Same general formula.
Neighbouring members differ by CH2 (in molecular formula).
Gradual variation / trend in physical properties, e.g. boiling point increases with chain length.
Similar chemical properties / react in the same way.
exam.tip: One mark per feature: learn them as a numbered list.

exam.q: Pentane (C5H12) boils at 36 °C and heptane (C7H16) boils at 98 °C. Predict the boiling point of hexane, C6H14, and explain your prediction.
model: Between 36 °C and 98 °C (actual 69 °C; accept about 60 to 75 °C).
Hexane has a chain length between pentane and heptane / boiling point increases gradually with number of carbon atoms.
exam.tip: Use the gradual-variation idea and give a value in the right range.

exam.q: Explain why the boiling points of the alkanes increase as the number of carbon atoms increases.
model: Molecules get larger / longer chains.
Intermolecular forces (between molecules) become stronger.
More (heat) energy is needed to overcome the forces.
exam.tip: Must say 'between molecules' or 'intermolecular'.

exam.q: Explain whether C5H10 is a member of the alkane homologous series.
model: No.
An alkane with 5 carbons would be C5H12 / C5H10 does not fit CnH2n+2 (it fits CnH2n, an alkene).
exam.tip: Show the substitution into the general formula.

exam.q: Butane and propane are both used as fuels in camping gas. Explain, using the idea of a homologous series, why they both release energy when burned and produce the same products.
model: They are in the same homologous series so have similar chemical properties.
Both undergo combustion to form carbon dioxide and water (releasing energy).
exam.tip: Name the feature (similar chemical properties) and give the reaction.

exam.q: An alkane has a relative formula mass of 142. Find its molecular formula. (Ar: C = 12, H = 1)
exam.tip: Mr of an alkane = 14n + 2; check: 120 + 22 = 142.

exam.q: Write a balanced equation for the complete combustion of propane.
model: 1 mark for correct formulae, 1 for balancing.
exam.tip: Balance C first, then H, then O last.

worked.q: An alkane molecule contains 26 hydrogen atoms. Find its molecular formula and its relative formula mass.
steps: General formula CnH2n+2, so 2n + 2 = 26.
Molecular formula C12H26.
Check with 14n + 2: 14 x 12 + 2 = 170. Correct.

worked.q: Butane boils at -1 °C, pentane at 36 °C and hexane at 69 °C. Predict the boiling point of heptane and its state at 25 °C.
steps: Differences: 36 - (-1) = 37; 69 - 36 = 33. The increase is getting slightly smaller.
Next increase is likely to be about 29 to 30 °C.
98 °C is above 25 °C, so heptane is a liquid at 25 °C.
worked.ans: About 98 °C (accept about 95 to 100 °C); liquid at 25 °C.

worked.q: Model answer: Use the data in the alkanes table to show that the alkanes form a homologous series.
steps: Same general formula: CH4, C2H6, C3H8 and C4H10 all fit CnH2n+2.
Differ by CH2: C2H6 - CH4 = CH2; C3H8 - C2H6 = CH2, and so on.
Gradual variation in physical properties: boiling point rises steadily from -162 °C (methane) to 69 °C (hexane).
Similar chemical properties: they all burn in oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water.
worked.ans: All four features are shown, so the alkanes are a homologous series.

chem_edx.8.3.summary: Hydrocarbons are used as fuels because they release a **large amount of energy** when they burn. In a **plentiful supply of oxygen**, **complete combustion** oxidises the carbon to **carbon dioxide** and the hydrogen to **water**. When oxygen is **limited**, **incomplete combustion** produces **carbon monoxide** and/or **carbon (soot)** as well as water, and releases less energy. Carbon monoxide is a toxic, colourless, odourless gas that stops the blood carrying oxygen, and soot causes breathing problems and blackens and blocks appliances.

core.h: Why hydrocarbons are used as fuels
core.p: A **fuel** is a substance that releases useful energy when it burns. Hydrocarbons such as methane (natural gas), petrol, kerosene and diesel are excellent fuels because their combustion is **strongly exothermic**: it releases a **large amount of energy** (as heat and light) for a small mass of fuel.
bullets: Hydrocarbons are used as fuels because of the **large amount of energy released** when they burn **completely**.
Combustion is **exothermic**: energy is transferred **to the surroundings**, so the temperature of the surroundings rises.
Burning a hydrocarbon is an **oxidation** reaction: the fuel **gains oxygen**.
Both elements in a hydrocarbon are oxidised: carbon to an oxide of carbon, hydrogen to water (hydrogen oxide).
Most fuels are obtained from **crude oil** or **natural gas**, which are finite resources.

callouts.p: Hydrocarbons are used as fuels because they release **a lot of energy** when they **burn** (combust) in oxygen.

core.p: **Complete combustion** happens when there is a **plentiful (excess) supply of oxygen** (air). All the carbon atoms are oxidised to **carbon dioxide** and all the hydrogen atoms are oxidised to **water**. This releases the **maximum** amount of energy from the fuel.
bullets: General word equation: **hydrocarbon + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water**.
Methane: CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O
Propane: C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O
Butane: 2C4H10 + 13O2 -> 8CO2 + 10H2O
Octane (in petrol): 2C8H18 + 25O2 -> 16CO2 + 18H2O
Gives a **clean blue flame** (e.g. a Bunsen burner with the air hole open).
Carbon dioxide is a **greenhouse gas**, linked to climate change (covered in 8.24-8.26).

callouts.p: Burning a fuel in a **plentiful supply of oxygen**, so that a hydrocarbon forms **only carbon dioxide and water**.
Balance **C first** (number of CO2), then **H** (number of H2O = H atoms / 2), then **O last**. If you need an odd number of O atoms, double everything.

core.p: **Oxidation** is the **gain of oxygen**. In combustion, oxygen from the air combines with both the carbon and the hydrogen in the fuel. That is why the products are **oxides**: carbon dioxide (an oxide of carbon) and water (an oxide of hydrogen).
bullets: C atoms in the fuel -> CO2: carbon has **gained oxygen** (oxidised).
H atoms in the fuel -> H2O: hydrogen has **gained oxygen** (oxidised).
In incomplete combustion the carbon is **less oxidised**: CO has less oxygen than CO2, and C (soot) has none.
Combustion needs fuel, oxygen and heat (the fire triangle) to start.

callouts.p: The **gain of oxygen** by a substance.

core.h: Testing the products of complete combustion
core.p: You can show that burning a hydrocarbon makes water and carbon dioxide. A **pump** draws the gases from a burning fuel through a cooled U-tube and then through **limewater**.
bullets: The **U-tube in ice** cools the gases so **water vapour condenses** to a colourless liquid.
Test for water: turns **anhydrous copper sulfate from white to blue** (or cobalt chloride paper from blue to pink).
Test that it is **pure** water: it **boils at 100 °C** (and freezes at 0 °C).
Test for carbon dioxide: bubble through **limewater**, which turns **milky / cloudy**.
A control tube with no flame shows that ordinary air turns limewater milky only very slowly.

callouts.p: Anhydrous copper sulfate shows water is **present**; only a boiling point of exactly 100 °C shows it is **pure** water.

core.p: **Incomplete combustion** happens when the supply of oxygen is **limited** (insufficient). There is not enough oxygen to turn all the carbon into carbon dioxide, so some carbon forms **carbon monoxide (CO)** or is released as **solid carbon particles (soot)**. Water is still formed, because hydrogen is oxidised more readily.
bullets: Products: **carbon monoxide** and/or **carbon (soot)**, plus **water** (and often some carbon dioxide).
Methane forming carbon monoxide: 2CH4 + 3O2 -> 2CO + 4H2O
Methane forming soot: CH4 + O2 -> C + 2H2O
Propane forming carbon monoxide: 2C3H8 + 7O2 -> 6CO + 8H2O
Propane forming soot: C3H8 + 2O2 -> 3C + 4H2O
Octane forming carbon monoxide: 2C8H18 + 17O2 -> 16CO + 18H2O
Gives a **yellow, smoky (sooty) flame**, e.g. a Bunsen burner with the air hole closed.
**Less energy is released** per gram of fuel than in complete combustion, so it wastes fuel.

callouts.p: Burning a fuel in a **limited (insufficient) supply of oxygen**, producing **carbon monoxide and/or carbon (soot)** as well as water.
There is **not enough oxygen** to fully oxidise all of the carbon to CO2, so some is only partly oxidised to **CO**, or not oxidised at all and left as **C**.

core.p: Think of the products as a sliding scale controlled by how much oxygen is available. The more oxygen, the more fully the carbon is oxidised and the more energy is released.
bullets: **Plenty** of oxygen: CO2 + H2O (complete).
**Limited** oxygen: CO + H2O (incomplete).
**Very little** oxygen: C (soot) + H2O (incomplete).
In real appliances a **mixture** of CO2, CO and C can form at the same time.
Long-chain fuels such as diesel and fuel oil are **more likely** to burn incompletely, as they need much more oxygen per molecule.

core.p: Carbon monoxide is **toxic** because it **combines with haemoglobin** in **red blood cells**. Haemoglobin normally carries oxygen around the body. CO binds to haemoglobin **more strongly than oxygen does**, so it **reduces the ability of the blood to carry oxygen**. Body tissues, especially the brain and heart, are starved of oxygen.
bullets: CO combines with **haemoglobin** in red blood cells.
This **reduces the amount of oxygen** the blood can carry.
Symptoms: headaches, dizziness, drowsiness, nausea, breathlessness, unconsciousness and eventually **death**.
CO is **colourless and odourless**, so it **cannot be detected** by our senses: you cannot see or smell it.
This is why homes with gas boilers, fires and cookers should have a **carbon monoxide detector** (alarm).
Faulty or badly ventilated appliances, and blocked flues, are the usual cause of CO poisoning.

callouts.p: CO **combines with haemoglobin** (in red blood cells), **reducing the capacity of the blood to carry oxygen**.
Do not say CO 'damages the lungs' or 'blocks the airways'. It acts in the **blood**, on **haemoglobin**.

core.p: **Soot** is fine particles of **carbon** produced by incomplete combustion. It causes problems for health, for appliances and for the environment.
bullets: **Health**: soot particles can be breathed in and cause **breathing problems** and **lung diseases**, and can make asthma worse; very fine particulates are linked to cancer.
**Appliances**: soot **blackens** buildings and appliances and can **block flues and chimneys**, which stops waste gases escaping and increases the risk of **carbon monoxide** build-up in the room.
**Efficiency**: soot coating a heat exchanger reduces heat transfer, so the appliance is **less efficient**; incomplete combustion itself also **releases less energy**.
**Environment**: soot in the atmosphere causes **global dimming** by reflecting sunlight, and darkens buildings.
Soot also shows that fuel is being **wasted**.

callouts.p: 'Soot is bad for the environment' scores nothing. Say **'causes breathing problems'**, **'blackens buildings'** or **'blocks flues'**.

core.h: Problems in appliances that burn carbon fuels
core.p: Edexcel asks about the problems of incomplete combustion in **appliances** that use carbon compounds as fuels, such as gas boilers, gas fires, cookers, wood burners and car engines. A yellow flame or soot marks around an appliance are warning signs.
bullets: Produces **toxic carbon monoxide**, which can build up indoors.
Produces **soot**, which blackens and blocks the appliance and flue.
Releases **less energy**, so it is less efficient and wastes fuel (higher cost).
Prevention: ensure **good ventilation** (plenty of air), have appliances **serviced regularly**, keep flues clear, and fit **CO alarms**.
A blue flame indicates the appliance is working correctly; a yellow or orange flame suggests a fault.

callouts.p: Carbon **dioxide** is not toxic in this way; carbon **monoxide** is. Check the formula you write: CO, not CO2.

core.p: Complete combustion releases **more energy** than incomplete combustion from the same amount of fuel. In incomplete combustion, some of the chemical energy stays in the CO and C, which could still burn further (CO can burn to CO2, releasing more energy).
bullets: 2CO + O2 -> 2CO2 releases energy, showing CO is only **partly oxidised**.
Soot (C) can burn: C + O2 -> CO2.
So incomplete combustion = **wasted energy** + **harmful products**.

core.p: For incomplete combustion the question tells you the carbon product. Balance carbon first, then hydrogen, then work out how much oxygen is needed. Because less oxygen is used, the O2 number is **smaller** than for complete combustion.
bullets: Step 1: write fuel + O2 -> CO (or C) + H2O.
Step 2: number of CO (or C) = number of C atoms in the fuel.
Step 3: number of H2O = H atoms / 2.
Step 4: count O atoms on the right and divide by 2 for O2; double everything if you get a half.
Example, ethane to CO: 2C2H6 + 5O2 -> 4CO + 6H2O (O: 4 + 6 = 10, so 5O2).

analogy.p: Think of each carbon atom in the fuel as a customer who must pay two oxygen atoms to leave the shop fully as CO2, and each pair of hydrogen atoms pays one oxygen atom to leave as H2O. When the shop has plenty of oxygen 'money', every customer pays in full: complete combustion, maximum energy. When oxygen runs short, the hydrogens pay first (water still forms), and some carbons can only pay one oxygen (leaving as CO) or none at all (left behind as soot). Where it breaks down: atoms do not take turns or 'choose'; the products depend on the conditions in the flame, and in reality a mixture of CO2, CO and C forms at the same time.

terms.d: A substance that releases useful energy when it burns.
A reaction in which a substance reacts with oxygen, releasing energy (burning).
Burning in a plentiful supply of oxygen; a hydrocarbon forms only carbon dioxide and water.
Burning in a limited supply of oxygen, producing carbon monoxide and/or carbon (soot) as well as water.
The gain of oxygen by a substance; combustion is an oxidation reaction.
A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, so the surroundings get hotter.
CO; a toxic, colourless, odourless gas formed by incomplete combustion.
Fine particles of carbon produced by incomplete combustion.
The protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen; carbon monoxide binds to it.
Poisonous; harmful to living organisms.
Calcium hydroxide solution, which turns milky (cloudy) when carbon dioxide is bubbled through it.
White solid that turns blue when water is added; a test for water.
Reduction in sunlight reaching the Earth's surface caused by particulates such as soot in the atmosphere.
A pipe or chimney that carries waste gases away from a boiler or fire.
An alarm that sounds when CO is present, needed because CO cannot be seen or smelled.

mistakes.w: Hydrocarbons burn to give carbon dioxide and hydrogen.
mistakes.r: Complete combustion gives **carbon dioxide and water**.

mistakes.w: Incomplete combustion happens when there is no oxygen.
mistakes.r: Incomplete combustion happens with a **limited / insufficient** supply of oxygen; with no oxygen there is no combustion.

mistakes.w: Carbon monoxide damages the lungs / blocks the airways.
mistakes.r: CO **combines with haemoglobin** in red blood cells, **reducing the oxygen-carrying capacity** of the blood.

mistakes.w: Carbon monoxide is dangerous because it is a greenhouse gas.
mistakes.r: CO is dangerous because it is **toxic** and **colourless and odourless**, so it cannot be detected.

mistakes.w: Soot is bad for the environment (no detail).
mistakes.r: Soot causes **breathing problems**, **blackens buildings** and **blocks flues**; it can cause global dimming.

mistakes.w: Incomplete combustion releases more energy because it is quicker.
mistakes.r: Incomplete combustion releases **less energy** than complete combustion.

mistakes.w: Limewater turns blue / cloudy with water.
mistakes.r: Limewater turns **milky** with **carbon dioxide**; water turns anhydrous copper sulfate **white to blue**.

mistakes.w: Writing CO2 when CO is meant (or vice versa).
mistakes.r: Carbon **monoxide** = **CO**; carbon **dioxide** = **CO2**.

mistakes.w: Combustion is a reduction reaction.
mistakes.r: Combustion is **oxidation**: the fuel gains oxygen.

exam.q: State why hydrocarbons are used as fuels.
model: They release a large amount of (heat) energy when they burn / are combusted.
exam.tip: 'They burn' alone is not enough: mention energy.

exam.q: Name the two products of the complete combustion of a hydrocarbon.
model: Carbon dioxide.
Water.
exam.tip: Not 'hydrogen' and not 'oxygen'.

exam.q: Write a balanced equation for the complete combustion of methane, CH4.
model: CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O
1 mark for correct formulae, 1 mark for balancing.
exam.tip: Check: 4 O atoms on each side.

exam.q: State the condition that causes incomplete combustion.
model: A limited / insufficient supply of oxygen (air).
exam.tip: Avoid 'no oxygen'.

exam.q: Give two products, other than water, that may form in the incomplete combustion of a hydrocarbon.
model: Carbon monoxide.
Carbon / soot (accept carbon dioxide only if both others not listed).
exam.tip: Name CO and C: these are the two the spec names.

exam.q: Explain why carbon monoxide is toxic.
model: It combines with haemoglobin (in red blood cells).
This reduces the ability of the blood to carry oxygen (around the body).
exam.tip: Name haemoglobin and the effect on oxygen transport.

exam.q: Explain why a carbon monoxide detector should be fitted in a room with a gas boiler.
model: Incomplete combustion in the boiler (e.g. if faulty or poorly ventilated) can produce carbon monoxide, which is toxic.
CO is colourless and odourless, so it cannot be detected by people without a detector.
exam.tip: Two linked ideas: how CO arises, and why you cannot detect it yourself.

exam.q: Describe two problems caused by soot from incomplete combustion.
model: Breathing problems / lung damage / asthma when inhaled.
Blackens buildings / appliances; or blocks flues/chimneys; or global dimming.
exam.tip: Give two different types of problem.

exam.q: Balance the equation for the incomplete combustion of propane: C3H8 + ...O2 -> 3C + ...H2O
exam.tip: H first: 8 H atoms -> 4 H2O, which needs 4 O atoms = 2O2.

exam.q: A student burns a hydrocarbon fuel and draws the gases through a cooled U-tube and then limewater. Describe what is observed and explain what the observations show.
model: A colourless liquid collects in the U-tube.
It turns anhydrous copper sulfate from white to blue, so it is water (boils at 100 °C if pure).
Limewater turns milky / cloudy.
This shows carbon dioxide is produced, so the fuel contains carbon and hydrogen / combustion is oxidation forming CO2 and H2O.
exam.tip: Pair each observation with its meaning.

exam.q: Compare complete and incomplete combustion of hydrocarbons, explaining the hazards associated with incomplete combustion.
model: Complete combustion occurs in a plentiful supply of oxygen; incomplete in a limited supply.
Complete: products are carbon dioxide and water only; incomplete: carbon monoxide and/or carbon (soot) and water.
Complete combustion releases more energy; incomplete releases less, so fuel is wasted.
Complete gives a blue flame; incomplete a yellow, smoky flame.
CO is toxic: it combines with haemoglobin, reducing the blood's ability to carry oxygen; it is colourless and odourless so is hard to detect.
Soot causes breathing problems, blackens buildings and can block flues (raising CO risk); CO2 from complete combustion is a greenhouse gas.
exam.tip: Structure as a direct comparison, then hazards. Use 'whereas' to link the two types.

worked.q: Write a balanced equation for the complete combustion of pentane, C5H12.
steps: Unbalanced: C5H12 + O2 -> CO2 + H2O
Carbon: 5 C atoms, so 5CO2.
Hydrogen: 12 H atoms, so 6H2O.
Oxygen on the right: (5 x 2) + 6 = 16 O atoms, so 8O2.
Check: left C5 H12 O16; right C5 H12 O16.

worked.q: Write a balanced equation for the incomplete combustion of butane, C4H10, forming carbon monoxide and water.
steps: Unbalanced: C4H10 + O2 -> CO + H2O
Carbon: 4CO.
Hydrogen: 10 H atoms, so 5H2O.
Oxygen on the right: 4 + 5 = 9 O atoms, which is 4.5 O2.
Double everything to remove the half: 2C4H10 + 9O2 -> 8CO + 10H2O.
Check: left C8 H20 O18; right C8 H20 O(8 + 10) = 18.

worked.q: Model answer: A family notices that their gas fire burns with a yellow flame and the wall above it is black. Explain the dangers and what they should do.
steps: A yellow flame and black marks (soot) show incomplete combustion, caused by a limited oxygen supply, e.g. a fault or blocked air vent/flue.
Incomplete combustion produces carbon monoxide, which is toxic: it combines with haemoglobin and reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood.
CO is colourless and odourless, so the family would not notice it.
Soot can block the flue, so waste gases (including CO) build up in the room, and soot can cause breathing problems.
They should stop using the fire, ventilate the room, have it serviced and fit a CO alarm.
worked.ans: Risk of carbon monoxide poisoning and soot-related breathing problems; switch off, ventilate, service the fire and fit a CO detector.

chem_edx.8.4.summary: Fossil fuels such as coal, diesel and petrol often contain **sulfur impurities**. When the fuel burns, the sulfur is oxidised to **sulfur dioxide**, which dissolves in rain water to form **acid rain**. Separately, the **very high temperatures in car engines** make nitrogen and oxygen from the air react to form **oxides of nitrogen (NOx)**, which are also pollutants that cause acid rain, smog and breathing problems. You must be able to explain how each pollutant forms, write the equations, describe the damage acid rain does and suggest ways of reducing these emissions.

core.p: Crude oil and coal formed from the remains of ancient living things. Proteins in those organisms contained sulfur, so many fossil fuels still contain **sulfur compounds as impurities**. Coal and the heavier fractions of crude oil (such as diesel and fuel oil) usually contain the most sulfur.
bullets: The sulfur is **not part of the hydrocarbon** itself: it is an **impurity** mixed in with the fuel.
Hydrocarbons contain only hydrogen and carbon, so a pure hydrocarbon cannot make sulfur dioxide.
Coal burned in power stations is a major source of sulfur dioxide.
Natural gas usually has very little sulfur once it has been processed.
Modern petrol and diesel are treated to remove most of the sulfur before sale (**desulfurisation**).

callouts.p: Sulfur dioxide comes from the **combustion of sulfur impurities** in the fuel, not from the carbon or hydrogen in the hydrocarbon.

core.p: When a fuel burns, every element in it reacts with oxygen. The carbon forms carbon dioxide, the hydrogen forms water, and any sulfur impurity is **oxidised** to sulfur dioxide gas, which leaves in the exhaust or chimney gases.
bullets: Word equation: sulfur + oxygen → sulfur dioxide
Symbol equation: S + O2 → SO2
Sulfur dioxide is a **colourless, toxic gas** with a sharp, choking smell.
It is an **acidic oxide**: it is a non-metal oxide, so it forms an acid when it dissolves in water.
It irritates the lungs and can make **asthma** and other breathing problems worse.
The combustion of sulfur is an **oxidation** reaction because sulfur gains oxygen.

callouts.p: Some hydrocarbon fuels contain sulfur impurities. When the fuel is burned, the sulfur reacts with oxygen to form sulfur dioxide: S + O2 → SO2.

core.h: How sulfur dioxide causes acid rain
core.p: Sulfur dioxide released into the air **dissolves in water droplets in clouds**. It reacts with the water (and with more oxygen) to form acids, mainly **sulfuric acid**. This falls as rain with a pH much lower than normal, which is called **acid rain**.
bullets: SO2 + H2O → H2SO3 (sulfurous acid)
Sulfurous acid is then oxidised in the air: 2H2SO3 + O2 → 2H2SO4 (sulfuric acid)
Overall: 2SO2 + O2 + 2H2O → 2H2SO4
At GCSE it is enough to say: **sulfur dioxide dissolves in rain water to form an acidic solution (sulfuric acid)**.
Clouds can carry the pollution hundreds of kilometres, so acid rain can fall in a different country from where the fuel was burned.
Acid rain is an example of pollution that does not respect borders, so it needs **international agreements** to control.

callouts.p: Always say the SO2 **dissolves in rain water** (or water in clouds). Saying it 'mixes with clouds' does not earn the mark.

core.p: Even clean rain is **slightly acidic** because carbon dioxide from the air dissolves in it to form a weak acid (carbonic acid). Its pH is about 5.6. Rain is called **acid rain** when its pH is lower than this, usually below about 5, because of dissolved sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen.
bullets: Pure water has pH 7 (neutral).
Unpolluted rain: about pH 5.6, due to dissolved CO2.
Acid rain: often pH 4 to 5, and sometimes lower.
Each drop of 1 on the pH scale means the solution is **10 times more acidic** (10 times greater H+ concentration).
So rain of pH 4.6 has about 10 times the hydrogen ion concentration of rain at pH 5.6.

core.h: Problems caused by acid rain: buildings and metals
core.p: Acid rain reacts with materials that react with acids. **Limestone and marble** are mainly **calcium carbonate**, which reacts with acids and slowly dissolves, so buildings and statues are **eroded** (weathered). Acid rain also speeds up the **corrosion of metals** such as iron and steel.
bullets: CaCO3 + H2SO4 → CaSO4 + H2O + CO2
Word equation: calcium carbonate + sulfuric acid → calcium sulfate + water + carbon dioxide
Carved details on old limestone churches and statues become blurred and crumble away.
Acid rain reacts with iron and steel in bridges, railways and car bodies, so they **corrode faster** and need more maintenance.
Metals react with acids: for example Fe + H2SO4 → FeSO4 + H2
These repairs cost a lot of money.

callouts.p: For full marks say that limestone is **calcium carbonate** and that it **reacts with the acid** in the rain, producing carbon dioxide.

core.h: Problems caused by acid rain: lakes, rivers and living things
core.p: When acid rain falls into lakes and rivers, the water becomes more acidic. Many aquatic organisms can only survive in a narrow pH range, so **fish, insects and plants die**, and food chains are disrupted. Acid rain also harms trees and soil.
bullets: Lakes and rivers become **too acidic for fish and other aquatic life** to survive; eggs and young fish are especially sensitive.
Acid rain **damages the leaves of trees** and can kill whole areas of forest.
Acidic soil loses nutrients (such as magnesium and calcium) because they are washed out, so plants grow poorly.
Acid water can release **toxic metal ions** (such as aluminium) from soil and rocks into rivers, which harms fish gills.
Damage to one species affects the rest of the **food chain**.
Lakes can be treated by adding powdered **limestone or lime** to neutralise the acid, but this is expensive and only treats the effect, not the cause.

head: What is affected
Problem caused by acid rain
rows: React with acid and are eroded
Become too acidic, fish and aquatic organisms die
Nutrients washed out, plant growth reduced

callouts.p: Acid rain: **damages buildings and statues made of limestone**, **corrodes metals**, and **harms living things** (kills fish and aquatic life, damages trees).

core.h: Oxides of nitrogen from car engines
core.p: Air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen. Nitrogen is very unreactive at normal temperatures because of its strong triple bond. However, inside a car engine the fuel burns at **very high temperatures**, which gives enough energy for **nitrogen and oxygen from the air to react** with each other. This produces **oxides of nitrogen**, written as **NOx**.
bullets: The nitrogen comes from the **air**, not from the fuel.
N2 + O2 → 2NO (nitrogen monoxide, also called nitric oxide)
The NO then reacts with more oxygen in the air: 2NO + O2 → 2NO2 (nitrogen dioxide)
Nitrogen dioxide is a **brown, toxic gas**.
The reaction needs a high temperature because a lot of energy is needed to **break the strong bonds** in nitrogen molecules.
Oxides of nitrogen are also produced in power stations and other high-temperature furnaces, and by lightning.

callouts.p: The high temperatures in car engines cause nitrogen and oxygen from the air to react, producing oxides of nitrogen, which are pollutants.
Hydrocarbon fuels do not contain nitrogen. Never write that NOx is formed 'when nitrogen in the petrol burns'.

core.h: Problems caused by oxides of nitrogen
core.p: Oxides of nitrogen are **pollutants** because they harm human health and the environment.
bullets: **Acid rain**: nitrogen dioxide dissolves in rain water (with oxygen) to form **nitric acid**: 4NO2 + O2 + 2H2O → 4HNO3
**Respiratory problems**: NO2 irritates the lungs and airways and makes **asthma** worse.
**Photochemical smog**: in sunlight, oxides of nitrogen react with other pollutants to form a brown haze over busy cities.
Nitrogen dioxide is toxic, so busy roads and city centres often have the worst NOx levels.
Diesel engines tend to produce more NOx than petrol engines because they run at higher temperatures and pressures.

head: Pollutant
Where it comes from
Main problems
rows: N2 and O2 from air reacting at high temperature in engines
Acid rain, photochemical smog, breathing problems

callouts.p: Sulfur dioxide forms **sulfuric acid** and oxides of nitrogen form **nitric acid** in rain water.

core.p: The best way to stop acid rain is to stop the pollutants reaching the air in the first place.
bullets: **Remove sulfur from fuels before burning** (desulfurisation): petrol and diesel sold in the UK are now low-sulfur fuels.

**Flue gas desulfurisation** in power stations: waste gases are passed through a 'scrubber' containing an alkaline or basic substance such as **calcium oxide** or **calcium carbonate** slurry, which reacts with and removes sulfur dioxide.
Burn fuels that contain less sulfur, such as natural gas instead of coal.
**Use less fossil fuel**: renewable energy (wind, solar), more efficient appliances and public transport.
In the UK, closing most coal-fired power stations has greatly reduced SO2 emissions and acid rain.

callouts.p: Sulfur dioxide is an **acidic** gas, so it is removed by reacting it with a **base** such as calcium oxide. This is a neutralisation-type reaction.

core.h: Reducing oxides of nitrogen: catalytic converters
core.p: Modern petrol cars are fitted with a **catalytic converter** in the exhaust. It contains a honeycomb coated with metals such as **platinum and rhodium**, giving a large surface area. The catalyst speeds up reactions that turn harmful gases into less harmful ones.
bullets: Oxides of nitrogen react with carbon monoxide: 2NO + 2CO → N2 + 2CO2
Nitrogen monoxide is **reduced** back to nitrogen gas, which is harmless and already makes up most of the air.
Carbon monoxide is oxidised to carbon dioxide at the same time.
The honeycomb structure gives a **large surface area** so the reactions are fast.
Catalytic converters only work well once they are **hot**, so short journeys still release pollutants.
They do not reduce carbon dioxide emissions (they actually turn CO into CO2).

callouts.t: Catalytic converters do not remove CO2
callouts.p: They convert NOx and CO into N2 and CO2. The car still releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas.
