core.h: Linking the ideas: why higher temperature and more fuel mean more pollution
core.p: Grade 9 answers connect cause and effect. More fuel burned means more sulfur impurity oxidised, so more SO2. Higher engine temperatures provide more energy to break the strong N≡N triple bond, so more NOx forms. More SO2 and NOx dissolved in rain gives a higher concentration of acid, a lower pH and more damage.
bullets: Amount of SO2 depends on **how much sulfur is in the fuel** and **how much fuel is burned**.
Amount of NOx depends mainly on **temperature** (and how much air is present), not on the fuel composition.
Traffic-heavy cities have high NOx; regions with coal power stations historically had high SO2.
Reducing pollution can be done at three stages: **before** burning (clean fuel), **during** (lower temperature, efficient engines) and **after** (scrubbers, catalytic converters).
Treating the damage (liming lakes, repairing buildings) is costly and does not remove the cause.

callouts.p: Source of pollutant → equation → dissolves in rain to form acid → named effects → how to reduce it. Cover both SO2 and NOx if the question says 'pollutants'.

analogy.p: Burning a fuel with sulfur impurities is like burning damp garden rubbish that has plastic hidden in it: the main fuel burns as expected, but the hidden extra (sulfur) turns into a nasty extra gas you never wanted. NOx is different: it is like a hairdryer so hot that it starts to scorch the air itself; the nitrogen and oxygen were always in the air, but the extreme heat finally forces them to react. Where it breaks down: plastic contains carbon too, and real NOx formation needs specific temperatures inside a closed engine, not just 'hot air'. Also, the pollution only becomes acid rain after it dissolves in water in clouds, which the analogy does not show.

terms.d: An unwanted substance mixed in with the main substance; in fuels, sulfur compounds are impurities.
A toxic, colourless, acidic gas formed when sulfur impurities in fuels react with oxygen during combustion.
Rain with a pH lower than normal rain (below about 5.6, often below 5) caused by sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen dissolving in rain water.
The strong acid formed when sulfur dioxide dissolves in rain water and is oxidised.
Pollutant gases such as nitrogen monoxide (NO) and nitrogen dioxide (NO2) formed when nitrogen and oxygen from the air react at high temperatures.
A colourless gas formed directly in hot engines: N2 + O2 → 2NO.
A brown, toxic gas formed when nitrogen monoxide reacts with oxygen; dissolves in rain to form nitric acid.
The acid formed when nitrogen dioxide dissolves in rain water with oxygen.
A substance released into the environment that harms living things or the environment.
The reaction of a fuel with oxygen, releasing energy; an oxidation reaction.
Gain of oxygen by a substance, for example sulfur forming sulfur dioxide.
An oxide, usually of a non-metal, that dissolves in water to form an acidic solution, for example SO2 and NO2.
Removing sulfur or sulfur compounds from a fuel before it is burned, or removing SO2 from waste gases.
Passing power station waste gases through a base such as calcium oxide or calcium carbonate to remove sulfur dioxide.
A device in a car exhaust containing platinum and rhodium catalysts that converts NOx and CO into N2 and CO2.
A brown haze of pollution formed when oxides of nitrogen react with other pollutants in sunlight.
The main compound in limestone and marble, which reacts with acid rain and is eroded.

mistakes.w: Sulfur dioxide is made when the hydrocarbon burns.
mistakes.r: Sulfur dioxide is made when **sulfur impurities** in the fuel react with oxygen; hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen.

mistakes.w: Oxides of nitrogen come from nitrogen in the petrol.
mistakes.r: Nitrogen and oxygen **from the air** react at the **high temperatures** in the engine.

mistakes.w: Carbon dioxide causes acid rain.
mistakes.r: Acid rain is caused by **sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen**; CO2 only makes rain slightly acidic (pH 5.6) and is linked to global warming.

mistakes.w: Acid rain causes global warming / the hole in the ozone layer.
mistakes.r: Acid rain damages buildings, metals, trees and aquatic life; it is not the cause of global warming.

mistakes.w: SO2 mixes with clouds to make acid rain.
mistakes.r: SO2 **dissolves in water** (rain water or water droplets in clouds) to form an acidic solution / sulfuric acid.

mistakes.w: Acid rain melts buildings.
mistakes.r: Acid rain **reacts with** calcium carbonate in limestone, so the stone is **eroded / dissolves**.

mistakes.w: Catalytic converters stop cars making CO2.
mistakes.r: They convert NOx to N2 and CO to CO2; CO2 is still released.

mistakes.w: The engine makes NOx because the fuel burns incompletely.
mistakes.r: NOx forms because of the **high temperature**, not because of incomplete combustion (which makes CO and soot).

mistakes.w: Acid rain kills fish because it is poisonous.
mistakes.r: Lakes become **too acidic** (low pH) for fish and other aquatic organisms to survive; toxic metal ions may also be released.

exam.q: Name the gas formed when sulfur impurities in a fuel are burned.
model: Sulfur dioxide / SO2
exam.tip: Give the name or the formula, not 'sulfur oxide'.

exam.q: Write the balanced equation for the combustion of sulfur.
model: S + O2 → SO2
exam.tip: This one is short and easy to balance. Learn it.

exam.q: Explain how burning coal in a power station can lead to acid rain.
model: Coal contains sulfur (impurities) which reacts with oxygen to form sulfur dioxide
Sulfur dioxide dissolves in rain water to form an acid (sulfuric acid)
exam.tip: Two links: formation of SO2, then dissolving in rain water.

exam.q: Explain why oxides of nitrogen are produced in car engines even though petrol does not contain nitrogen.
model: The temperature in the engine is very high
Nitrogen and oxygen from the air react together (to form NO / NOx)
exam.tip: Must mention both 'high temperature' and 'from the air'.

exam.q: Give two problems caused by acid rain.
model: Damages/erodes buildings or statues made of limestone/marble
Kills fish or aquatic life / makes lakes too acidic
Damages trees/forests
Corrodes metal structures
exam.tip: Any two. Be specific: 'damages buildings' is fine but 'damages the environment' is too vague.

exam.q: Limestone statues are damaged by acid rain. Explain why, including a word equation.
model: Limestone is (mainly) calcium carbonate
Calcium carbonate reacts with the acid in the rain (so the stone is eroded)
calcium carbonate + sulfuric acid → calcium sulfate + water + carbon dioxide
exam.tip: Name the compound and use 'reacts' rather than 'melts'.

exam.q: Nitrogen monoxide, NO, reacts with oxygen to form nitrogen dioxide. Write a balanced equation for this reaction.
model: Correct formulae NO, O2 and NO2
Balanced: 2NO + O2 → 2NO2
exam.tip: Count the oxygen atoms: 2 + 2 on the left, 4 on the right.

exam.q: Unpolluted rain water has a pH of about 5.6. Explain why it is slightly acidic.
model: Carbon dioxide (in the air) dissolves in rain water
forming a weak acid (carbonic acid)
exam.tip: Keep this separate from acid rain, which is caused by SO2 and NOx.

exam.q: Describe two ways of reducing the amount of sulfur dioxide released into the atmosphere.
model: Remove sulfur from fuels before they are burned / use low-sulfur fuels
Remove SO2 from waste gases at power stations, e.g. react with calcium oxide/calcium carbonate
Burn less fossil fuel / use renewable energy sources
exam.tip: Any two distinct methods.

exam.q: Explain how a catalytic converter reduces the emission of oxides of nitrogen.
model: Contains a catalyst (platinum/rhodium) on a honeycomb with large surface area
Nitrogen monoxide reacts with carbon monoxide
producing nitrogen (and carbon dioxide), which are less harmful: 2NO + 2CO → N2 + 2CO2
exam.tip: Say what NO is converted into: nitrogen gas.

exam.q: Sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen are both pollutants produced by burning fuels. Explain how each is formed and the problems they cause.
model: Some fuels contain sulfur impurities
Sulfur reacts with oxygen when the fuel burns: S + O2 → SO2
High temperatures in car engines cause nitrogen and oxygen from the air to react
forming oxides of nitrogen: N2 + O2 → 2NO, then NO2
Both dissolve in rain water to form acids (sulfuric acid and nitric acid), giving acid rain
Acid rain erodes limestone buildings/statues, corrodes metals, damages trees and makes lakes too acidic for fish
NOx/SO2 also cause breathing problems / asthma; NOx contributes to photochemical smog
exam.tip: Level 3 answers cover both pollutants, how each forms, and at least two specific effects, in a logical order.

worked.q: A sample of coal contains 1.6 g of sulfur. Calculate the mass of sulfur dioxide formed when all of this sulfur burns. (Ar: S = 32, O = 16)
steps: Equation: S + O2 → SO2, so 1 mol S gives 1 mol SO2
Moles of S = 1.6 / 32 = 0.050 mol
worked.ans: 3.2 g of sulfur dioxide (the mass of SO2 is double the mass of sulfur burned).

worked.q: A city has a lot of diesel traffic and its rain has a pH of 4.6. Explain where the acidity comes from and compare it with normal rain.
steps: Engines run at high temperatures, so nitrogen and oxygen from the air react: N2 + O2 → 2NO
NO reacts with more oxygen: 2NO + O2 → 2NO2
NO2 dissolves in rain water (with oxygen) to form nitric acid
Any sulfur impurities in fuel form SO2, which forms sulfuric acid in rain
Normal rain is about pH 5.6; pH 4.6 is 1 unit lower, so the hydrogen ion concentration is about 10 times greater
worked.ans: The rain is acidic mainly because of nitric acid from NOx (plus sulfuric acid from SO2), and it is about 10 times more acidic than normal rain.

worked.q: Model answer: evaluate liming a lake compared with fitting scrubbers to a power station as ways to deal with acid rain.
steps: Liming adds calcium carbonate/calcium hydroxide to neutralise acid in the lake, quickly raising the pH so fish can survive
But it treats only that one lake and must be repeated, so the cost keeps going
It does nothing for buildings, trees or other lakes downwind
Scrubbers remove SO2 from waste gases before it is released, using calcium oxide or calcium carbonate
This stops acid rain forming at the source, protecting every area downwind
Scrubbers are expensive to install, but they deal with the cause
worked.ans: Scrubbers are the better long-term solution because they prevent the pollutant forming acid rain at all, whereas liming only treats the symptoms in one place.

chem_edx.8.5.summary: Hydrogen can replace petrol as a car fuel, either burned in an engine or used in a fuel cell. Its big advantage is that the **only product of its combustion is water**, so no carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, soot or sulfur dioxide is released from the car, and it releases **much more energy per kilogram** than petrol. However, hydrogen is a gas that is **hard to store and transport**, is highly flammable, has **few filling stations**, and is often made using energy from fossil fuels, so its overall benefit depends on how it is produced. You must be able to **evaluate** both fuels, giving advantages and disadvantages and reaching a justified conclusion.

core.h: What the spec asks you to do
core.p: This point asks you to **evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of using hydrogen, rather than petrol, as a fuel in cars**. 'Evaluate' means you must weigh up both sides and come to a **justified conclusion**, not just list facts.
bullets: Compare the **products of combustion** of each fuel.
Compare **energy released** per kilogram and the ease of storage.
Consider how each fuel is **obtained** (is it renewable or finite?).
Consider **safety**, **cost** and **infrastructure** (filling stations, car design).
Finish with a conclusion that links back to the evidence.

callouts.p: A top answer gives at least two advantages, at least two disadvantages, and a conclusion that starts 'Overall...' with a reason.

core.p: Petrol is a **fraction from the fractional distillation of crude oil**. It is a mixture of **hydrocarbons**, mostly alkanes with about 5 to 10 carbon atoms (octane, C8H18, is often used as an example). It has been the main car fuel for over a century.
bullets: Complete combustion of octane: 2C8H18 + 25O2 → 16CO2 + 18H2O
Word equation: petrol + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water
In a limited supply of oxygen, **incomplete combustion** produces **carbon monoxide** (toxic) and **soot** (carbon particles).
Any **sulfur impurities** form **sulfur dioxide** (acid rain).
High engine temperatures make **oxides of nitrogen** from the air.
Petrol comes from crude oil, which is **finite** and **non-renewable**.

callouts.p: Burning petrol releases **carbon dioxide** (greenhouse gas), and can release **carbon monoxide, soot, sulfur dioxide, oxides of nitrogen** and unburnt hydrocarbons.

core.p: Hydrogen, H2, is a **colourless, very flammable gas**. It reacts with oxygen to form **water only**. It can be used in cars in two ways: **burned in an internal combustion engine**, or **reacted in a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell** that produces electricity to drive an electric motor.
bullets: Word equation: hydrogen + oxygen → water
Symbol equation: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O
The reaction is **exothermic**: it releases a lot of energy.
There is **no carbon** in hydrogen, so it cannot make CO2, CO or soot.
Hydrogen contains **no sulfur**, so no SO2 is produced.
A fuel cell uses the same overall reaction but releases energy as **electricity** rather than heat.

callouts.p: Hydrogen burns in oxygen to produce water only: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O.

fig.cap: Comparing the products: hydrogen produces only water, while petrol produces carbon dioxide and water and can also release carbon monoxide, soot, oxides of nitrogen and sulfur dioxide.

core.h: Advantage 1: cleaner products at the point of use
core.p: Because hydrogen contains no carbon, **no carbon dioxide** is produced when it is used in the car. This means no contribution to the **greenhouse effect** from the exhaust, and no **carbon monoxide** or **soot** to harm health.
bullets: Water vapour is the **only product** of hydrogen combustion.
No CO2 from the exhaust, so less contribution to **climate change**.
No CO (toxic: it reduces the blood's ability to carry oxygen).
No soot particulates (which cause breathing problems and global dimming).
No SO2, so no contribution to **acid rain** from sulfur.
Much better **local air quality** in towns and cities.

callouts.p: If hydrogen is **burned** in an engine, the high temperature can still make nitrogen and oxygen from the air react to form **oxides of nitrogen**. A fuel cell does not produce NOx because it works at a lower temperature without a flame.

core.h: Advantage 2: more energy per kilogram, and a renewable source
core.p: Hydrogen releases about **three times as much energy per kilogram** as petrol, so less mass of fuel is needed. Hydrogen can also be made from **water**, which is plentiful, so it can be a **renewable** fuel, unlike petrol which comes from finite crude oil.
bullets: Energy released: hydrogen about 140 MJ per kg; petrol about 46 MJ per kg (approximate values).
Hydrogen can be produced by the **electrolysis of water**: 2H2O → 2H2 + O2
If the electricity comes from **renewable sources** (wind, solar, hydroelectric), the whole process can release very little CO2.
The water produced when hydrogen burns returns to the environment, so the raw material is not used up.
Petrol is made from crude oil, which is **non-renewable**: it is being used up much faster than it forms.

callouts.p: Per kilogram, hydrogen releases **more energy** than petrol. Per litre (by volume), it releases **much less**, because it is a gas with a very low density.

core.p: Hydrogen is a **gas** at room temperature with a **very low density**, so a large volume is needed to store enough fuel. To fit enough in a car it must be **compressed to very high pressure** or **cooled to a liquid** at about -253 °C. Petrol, by contrast, is a liquid that is easy to store in a simple, light tank.
bullets: High-pressure tanks must be **strong, thick and heavy**, which adds mass and cost to the car.
The tank takes up more space than a petrol tank holding the same energy.
Liquefying hydrogen needs a lot of energy to cool it.
Hydrogen molecules are tiny and can **leak** through seals and some materials.
Petrol stores and transports easily in tankers and underground tanks at normal pressure.

callouts.p: Don't just write 'hard to store'. Say it is a **gas**, so it must be stored **under high pressure** or as a liquid at **very low temperature**.

core.p: Hydrogen is **highly flammable** and forms explosive mixtures with air over a wide range of concentrations, so leaks are dangerous. There are also **very few hydrogen filling stations**, and hydrogen cars are expensive, whereas petrol stations are everywhere.
bullets: Hydrogen-air mixtures can **explode** if ignited (the 'squeaky pop' test shows this on a small scale).
Petrol is also flammable, but as a liquid its vapour is easier to contain.
Building a network of hydrogen filling stations would cost a lot of money.
Hydrogen fuel-cell cars are currently **more expensive** to buy than petrol cars.
Existing petrol engines cannot simply run on hydrogen without modification.

core.p: Hydrogen is not found naturally as a gas on Earth, so it has to be **manufactured**, and this needs energy. At present most hydrogen is made from **natural gas (methane)** or by **electrolysis** using electricity that may come from **fossil-fuel power stations**. In those cases carbon dioxide is still released, just at the factory or power station instead of from the car.
bullets: Making hydrogen from methane releases CO2 and uses a **non-renewable** resource.
Electrolysis of water needs a lot of **electrical energy**.
If that electricity comes from burning fossil fuels, CO2 is produced at the power station.
Hydrogen is only truly 'clean' if it is made using **renewable energy**.
This is why hydrogen is called an **energy carrier** rather than a primary energy source.

callouts.t: 'Hydrogen cars produce no pollution at all'
callouts.p: This is only true **at the car**. The overall pollution depends on **how the hydrogen was made**. Examiners reward students who point this out.

fig.cap: The ideal hydrogen fuel cycle: renewable electricity splits water by electrolysis, the hydrogen is stored and used in a car, and the water produced returns to the environment, so very little carbon dioxide is released overall.

core.p: Use this table to structure evaluation answers. Each row is a criterion: say which fuel is better for that criterion and why.
bullets: Hydrogen wins on: **products** (only water), **energy per kg**, **renewable** source (if made from water using renewable electricity).
Petrol wins on: **ease of storage**, **energy per litre**, **existing filling stations**, **cheaper cars**, **established technology**.
The **production method** of hydrogen is the deciding factor for its environmental benefit.

head: Criterion
Hydrogen
Petrol
rows: CO2, H2O; also CO, soot, SO2, NOx
Gas: high pressure or very cold liquid
Liquid: easy to store in a light tank

core.p: A **hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell** combines hydrogen and oxygen to make water and produce **electricity** directly, which then powers an electric motor. This is often how hydrogen cars actually work.
bullets: Overall reaction: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O (same as combustion).
No flame, so **no oxides of nitrogen** and the cell is quiet.
Fuel cells are **more efficient** than burning the fuel in an engine, as less energy is wasted as heat.
Fuel cells contain expensive catalysts such as platinum.
Fuel cells are covered in more detail in Topic 7 (triple chemistry); here you only need them as a way of using hydrogen in cars.

core.p: Examiners want a conclusion supported by evidence. A strong conclusion recognises that hydrogen is **better for the environment at the point of use** but that **practical problems** and the **production method** currently limit it.
bullets: Example: 'Overall, hydrogen is a better fuel for reducing pollution because it produces only water, but only if it is made by electrolysis using renewable electricity.'
Then add the limitation: 'At present petrol is more practical because it is a liquid that is easy to store and there are many filling stations.'
Always connect each point to a consequence (for example: no CO2 → does not add to the greenhouse effect).
Avoid one-word points such as 'cleaner' or 'cheaper' without explanation.

callouts.p: Judgement + main reason + condition or limitation.

analogy.t: Hydrogen is like a rechargeable battery for chemical energy
analogy.p: Petrol is like a disposable battery dug out of the ground: easy to use and carry, but once it is used it is gone and it leaves waste (CO2) behind. Hydrogen is like a rechargeable battery: you 'charge' it by putting energy in to split water, then 'discharge' it in the car and get water back, ready to be charged again. If you charge it from a solar panel the cycle is clean; if you charge it from a coal power station the pollution just happens somewhere else. Where it breaks down: a real battery stores energy in a solid package, while hydrogen is a gas that needs a heavy high-pressure tank, and no material is physically returned to the car after use.

terms.d: A substance that reacts (usually with oxygen) to release useful energy.
A colourless, highly flammable gas, H2, that burns in oxygen to form only water.
A fraction of crude oil, a mixture of hydrocarbons (mostly alkanes) used as fuel in cars.
Burning a fuel in plenty of oxygen; for a hydrocarbon the products are carbon dioxide and water.
Burning a hydrocarbon in a limited supply of oxygen, producing carbon monoxide and/or soot as well as water.
A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings, as in the combustion of fuels.
Using electricity to break down a compound; water can be electrolysed to make hydrogen and oxygen.
A resource that is replaced at least as fast as it is used, so it will not run out.
A resource being used up faster than it can be formed, such as crude oil.
A device in which a fuel such as hydrogen reacts with oxygen to produce electricity directly.
A gas, such as carbon dioxide, that absorbs infrared radiation and contributes to global warming.
A toxic gas from incomplete combustion that reduces the blood's ability to carry oxygen.
Pollutant gases formed when nitrogen and oxygen from the air react at the high temperatures in engines.
The energy released per unit mass of fuel; hydrogen's is about three times petrol's.
The network of facilities needed to supply a fuel, such as filling stations, pipelines and tankers.
Weigh up advantages and disadvantages and give a judgement supported by evidence.

mistakes.w: Hydrogen cars produce no pollution at all.
mistakes.r: No CO2, CO, soot or SO2 is produced **at the car**, but making the hydrogen may release CO2 if fossil fuels are used; burning hydrogen can also make NOx.

mistakes.w: Hydrogen produces carbon dioxide and water.
mistakes.r: Hydrogen contains **no carbon**, so the **only product is water**: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O.

mistakes.w: Hydrogen is hard to store.
mistakes.r: Hydrogen is a **gas**, so it has to be stored at **high pressure** or as a **liquid at very low temperature**, needing heavy, strong tanks.

mistakes.w: Hydrogen is renewable so it is always better.
mistakes.r: Hydrogen is only renewable/low carbon if it is made from water using **renewable electricity**; most is made from methane.

mistakes.w: Hydrogen releases less energy than petrol.
mistakes.r: Hydrogen releases **more energy per kilogram** than petrol (it releases less per litre because it is a gas).

mistakes.w: Petrol is renewable because we can make more of it.
mistakes.r: Petrol comes from **crude oil**, a **finite, non-renewable** resource formed over millions of years.

mistakes.w: 2H + O → H2O
mistakes.r: Hydrogen and oxygen are diatomic: **2H2 + O2 → 2H2O**.

mistakes.w: Hydrogen is better because it is cheaper.
mistakes.r: Hydrogen cars and hydrogen production are currently **more expensive**; there are few filling stations.

mistakes.w: Evaluation answer lists facts with no conclusion.
mistakes.r: An evaluation must end with a **justified conclusion** comparing the two fuels.

exam.q: Give the only product formed when hydrogen burns in air.
model: Water / H2O
exam.tip: Not 'water and carbon dioxide': there is no carbon in hydrogen.

exam.q: Write a balanced equation for the combustion of hydrogen.
model: Correct formulae: H2, O2, H2O
Balanced: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O
exam.tip: Remember both hydrogen and oxygen are diatomic.

exam.q: State one advantage of using hydrogen rather than petrol as a fuel for cars.
model: Only water is produced / no carbon dioxide produced
Releases more energy per kg
Can be made from water, a renewable resource
exam.tip: Any one. Be specific about the product.

exam.q: Explain why using hydrogen as a fuel does not contribute to global warming from the car exhaust.
model: Hydrogen contains no carbon (only product is water)
so no carbon dioxide (a greenhouse gas) is produced
exam.tip: Link 'no carbon' to 'no CO2' to 'no greenhouse gas'.

exam.q: Give two disadvantages of using hydrogen as a fuel in cars.
model: It is a gas so difficult to store / needs high pressure tanks or very low temperature
Highly flammable / explosive
Few filling stations
Production uses a lot of energy / often uses fossil fuels
Hydrogen cars are expensive
exam.tip: Any two distinct points.

exam.q: Hydrogen can be made by the electrolysis of water. Explain why hydrogen made this way may still lead to carbon dioxide emissions.
model: Electrolysis needs (a lot of) electricity
The electricity may be generated by burning fossil fuels, which releases carbon dioxide
exam.tip: Point out the pollution moves to the power station.

exam.q: Write a balanced equation for the complete combustion of octane, C8H18.
model: Correct products CO2 and H2O
exam.tip: Balance C, then H, then O; double everything if you get a half.

exam.q: Explain why burning petrol in a car engine can produce carbon monoxide but burning hydrogen cannot.
model: Petrol contains carbon; incomplete combustion (limited oxygen) produces carbon monoxide
Hydrogen contains no carbon, so no carbon monoxide can form
exam.tip: Mention 'incomplete combustion' for petrol.

exam.q: Hydrogen releases about 140 MJ per kg and petrol about 46 MJ per kg. Suggest why cars still use petrol tanks that are smaller than hydrogen tanks for the same journey.
model: Hydrogen is a gas with a very low density
so a much larger volume is needed / petrol is a liquid and stores more energy per litre
exam.tip: Distinguish energy per kg from energy per volume.

exam.q: Evaluate the use of hydrogen rather than petrol as a fuel for cars.
model: Hydrogen produces only water when it burns: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O
so no CO2 (greenhouse gas), CO (toxic), soot or SO2 are released from the car
Hydrogen releases more energy per kg than petrol
Hydrogen can be made from water (renewable), whereas petrol comes from crude oil (finite)
But hydrogen is a gas, hard to store: high pressure/heavy tanks or very low temperature
Very flammable/explosive; few filling stations; expensive cars
Hydrogen production uses energy, often from fossil fuels, so CO2 may still be released
Conclusion: hydrogen is better environmentally only if made using renewable energy; petrol currently more practical
exam.tip: Level 3 needs both sides and a justified conclusion.

worked.q: Calculate the mass of water produced when 4.0 g of hydrogen burns completely. (Ar: H = 1, O = 16)
steps: Equation: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O, so 2 mol H2 gives 2 mol H2O (ratio 1 : 1)
Mr of H2 = 2, so moles of H2 = 4.0 / 2 = 2.0 mol
Moles of H2O = 2.0 mol
Mr of H2O = 2 + 16 = 18
Mass of H2O = 2.0 × 18 = 36 g
worked.ans: 36 g of water.

worked.q: A hydrogen car needs 700 MJ of energy for a long journey. Hydrogen releases 140 MJ per kg and petrol releases 46 MJ per kg. Compare the masses of each fuel needed.
steps: Mass of hydrogen = 700 / 140 = 5.0 kg
Mass of petrol = 700 / 46 = 15.2 kg (3 s.f.)
Ratio: 15.2 / 5.0 = about 3 times more petrol by mass
But 5 kg of hydrogen gas takes up a far larger volume than 15 kg of liquid petrol unless it is highly compressed
worked.ans: About 5.0 kg of hydrogen versus about 15.2 kg of petrol: hydrogen is lighter for the same energy, but needs a large high-pressure tank.

worked.q: Model answer: A council wants to switch its buses from petrol to hydrogen. Evaluate this plan.
steps: For: buses would release only water, improving air quality in the town (no CO, soot or NOx from fuel cells)
For: no CO2 from the exhaust, so less contribution to climate change
For: hydrogen can be made from water, so it does not use up finite crude oil
Against: hydrogen must be stored at high pressure, so tanks are heavy and expensive
Against: the council would need to build its own hydrogen filling station
Against: if the hydrogen is made using fossil-fuel electricity or from methane, CO2 is still produced
Conclusion: worthwhile if the hydrogen is produced using renewable electricity, because the buses return to one depot to refuel, solving the filling station problem
worked.ans: Overall a good plan if the hydrogen comes from renewable electricity, because it removes local pollution and CO2, and a single depot overcomes the lack of filling stations.

chem_edx.8.6.summary: Coal, crude oil and natural gas are **fossil fuels**: they formed from the remains of ancient living things over **millions of years**. Because they form far more slowly than we use them, they are **non-renewable** and their supply is **finite**. You must recall that **petrol, kerosene and diesel oil** are non-renewable fossil fuels obtained from **crude oil**, and that **methane** is a non-renewable fossil fuel found in **natural gas**, and be able to explain why this matters and what the alternatives are.

core.p: For this point you must **recall** that **petrol, kerosene and diesel oil are non-renewable fossil fuels obtained from crude oil**, and that **methane is a non-renewable fossil fuel found in natural gas**. Grade 9 answers also explain **why** they are non-renewable and the consequences of using them.
bullets: Know the three main fossil fuels: **coal, crude oil and natural gas**.
Know which fuels come from crude oil: **petrol, kerosene, diesel oil** (plus others such as fuel oil and LPG).
Know that **methane, CH4**, is the main compound in natural gas.
Be able to define **non-renewable** and **finite**.
Be able to explain why fossil fuels cannot be replaced on a human timescale.

callouts.p: **Petrol, kerosene and diesel oil are non-renewable fossil fuels obtained from crude oil, and methane is a non-renewable fossil fuel found in natural gas.**

core.p: A **fossil fuel** is a fuel formed from the **remains of ancient living organisms** that were buried and changed by **heat and pressure** over **millions of years**. They store chemical energy that originally came from the Sun through photosynthesis.
bullets: **Coal**: formed mainly from the remains of **plants** (ancient forests and swamps).
**Crude oil**: formed mainly from the remains of tiny **sea creatures (plankton)** buried in mud.
**Natural gas**: formed in the same way as crude oil and often found trapped above it; it is mainly **methane**.
The remains were buried quickly, with **little or no oxygen**, so they did not fully decay.
Layers of sediment built up on top, increasing the **pressure** and **temperature** over time.
All fossil fuels contain carbon, so burning them releases **carbon dioxide**.

callouts.p: A fuel such as coal, crude oil or natural gas formed over millions of years from the remains of dead organisms under heat and pressure.

core.p: A resource is **non-renewable** when it is being **used up much faster than it can be replaced**. Fossil fuels took millions of years to form, but we are burning them in a few hundred years. Once used, they cannot be replaced on a human timescale, so their supply is **finite**: it will eventually run out.
bullets: **Finite** means there is a **limited amount**.
Some fossil fuels are still forming today, but **extremely slowly**, far slower than the rate we use them.
As easy-to-reach reserves run out, the remaining fuels become **harder and more expensive** to extract (deep sea, oil sands, fracking).
Demand keeps increasing as population and industry grow.
This is why scientists look for **renewable alternatives** and ways to **use less** fossil fuel.

callouts.p: A resource that is being used up faster than it is being formed, so it will run out.

callouts.t: 'They are not being made any more'
callouts.p: Not quite. Fossil fuels **are still forming**, but over **millions of years**, so the rate is far too slow to replace what we use.

core.p: Crude oil is a **complex mixture of hydrocarbons**. It is separated by **fractional distillation** into fractions with similar boiling points. Several of these fractions are important fuels, and because crude oil is non-renewable, **these fuels are non-renewable too**.
bullets: **Petrol**: fuel for cars; small molecules, low boiling point, very flammable.
**Kerosene**: fuel for aircraft (jet fuel), also used in some heaters and lamps.
**Diesel oil**: fuel for lorries, buses, trains, tractors and some cars.
Other fractions include **gases** (LPG, bottled gas for cooking and heating), **fuel oil** (ships, some power stations) and **bitumen** (roads and roofs, not a fuel).
Each fraction is a **mixture** of hydrocarbons, mostly **alkanes**, not a single compound.

callouts.p: Write **kerosene** (not paraffin) and **diesel oil** as the spec does. Bitumen is a crude oil fraction but **not a fuel**.

core.h: How the crude oil fuels differ
core.p: Petrol, kerosene and diesel oil are all hydrocarbon mixtures, but their molecules are different sizes. This links to fractional distillation (8.3-8.5): bigger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces, so higher boiling points.
bullets: Petrol has the **smallest molecules** of the three, the **lowest boiling point** and is the **most flammable**.
Kerosene molecules are larger than petrol molecules.
Diesel oil has the **largest molecules** of the three, the highest boiling point and is the most **viscous**.
Roughly: petrol about 5 to 10 carbon atoms, kerosene about 10 to 16, diesel oil about 14 to 20 (approximate ranges).
All three release **carbon dioxide and water** on complete combustion.

core.p: **Natural gas** is found trapped in rocks, often above crude oil deposits. It is mostly **methane, CH4**, the simplest alkane. Methane is a non-renewable fossil fuel because natural gas is finite.
bullets: Methane is the first member of the **alkane** homologous series (CnH2n+2 with n = 1).
It is piped to homes for **heating and cooking**, and burned in **power stations** to generate electricity.
Complete combustion: CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O
Incomplete combustion can produce **carbon monoxide** (dangerous in faulty gas boilers).
Methane is also a powerful **greenhouse gas** if it leaks unburned.
**Biogas** methane made from rotting waste is renewable, but **methane from natural gas** is a fossil fuel and non-renewable.

callouts.p: The spec says methane **found in natural gas** is non-renewable. Methane made by bacteria from waste (biogas) is renewable. Read the question carefully.

core.p: **Coal** is a solid fossil fuel formed from the remains of **plants** that grew in swampy forests hundreds of millions of years ago. Like oil and gas it is non-renewable and finite.
bullets: Coal is mostly **carbon**, with some hydrogen and impurities such as **sulfur**.
It is burned in power stations and used in making iron and steel.
Burning coal releases the most carbon dioxide per unit of energy of the three fossil fuels.
Coal often contains sulfur, so burning it can release **sulfur dioxide**, which causes acid rain (see 8.11-8.13).
The UK has closed almost all its coal-fired power stations to cut emissions.

core.h: Why fossil fuels are so widely used
core.p: Despite being finite and polluting, fossil fuels are used because they have many practical advantages. Understanding this helps when you evaluate alternatives.
bullets: They release **a lot of energy** when burned (highly exothermic).
They are **reliable**: power stations can generate electricity whenever it is needed, unlike wind or solar.
Liquid fuels such as petrol, kerosene and diesel are easy to **store and transport**.
There is a huge **existing infrastructure** (pipelines, refineries, filling stations, engines).
Crude oil is also a vital **feedstock** for the petrochemical industry (plastics, solvents, medicines, detergents), another reason not to waste it.

callouts.p: Crude oil is a **finite** source of both **fuels** and **chemicals**. Burning it as fuel means less is left to make plastics and other products.

core.p: Because fossil fuels are finite and their combustion releases pollutants, continuing to rely on them has economic and environmental consequences.
bullets: Reserves will **run out**, and prices rise as supplies become harder to extract.
Burning releases **carbon dioxide**, a greenhouse gas linked to **climate change**.
Incomplete combustion releases **carbon monoxide** and **soot**.
Sulfur impurities form **sulfur dioxide**; high-temperature engines form **oxides of nitrogen**: both cause **acid rain**.
Extracting fuels can damage habitats (oil spills, mining).

core.h: Renewable alternatives and conserving fossil fuels
core.p: To make finite fuels last longer and reduce pollution, we can **use less** and switch to **renewable** sources that will not run out.
bullets: **Renewable** fuels and energy sources: hydrogen made using renewable electricity, **biofuels** (bioethanol, biodiesel), biogas, wind, solar, hydroelectric, tidal, geothermal.
Use more fuel-efficient vehicles, electric or hybrid cars, and public transport.
Insulate homes so less gas is burned for heating.
**Crack** large, less useful hydrocarbons into smaller, more useful ones such as petrol, so less crude oil is wasted (8.16-8.17).
Recycle plastics, which saves crude oil used as feedstock.

callouts.p: A resource that can be replaced as fast as it is used, so it will not run out.

core.p: Questions on this point are usually short recall questions, but they are often combined with combustion, pollution or fractional distillation in longer answers.
bullets: If asked 'why is crude oil non-renewable', give **both** ideas: it takes **millions of years to form** and it is being **used faster than it forms**.
If asked to name fuels from crude oil, choose from **petrol, kerosene, diesel oil** (and fuel oil, LPG).
If asked what natural gas is mainly made of: **methane, CH4**.
Do not confuse **non-renewable** (cannot be replaced quickly) with **non-recyclable**.
Link 'finite' to consequences: supplies will run out, so we need alternatives.

callouts.p: Mark 1: takes millions of years to form. Mark 2: being used up faster than it is formed / will run out.

analogy.t: A savings account you cannot pay into
analogy.p: Fossil fuels are like a huge savings account that was filled up slowly over millions of years, a penny at a time. We are now withdrawing hundreds of pounds a day. Technically a penny still trickles in now and then (fuels are still forming), but compared with how fast we spend, it is nothing, so the account will eventually be empty: that is what finite and non-renewable mean. Renewable energy is more like a salary that keeps arriving. Where it breaks down: money can be earned back, but fossil fuels cannot be remade by humans on any useful scale, and spending this 'money' also produces pollution such as carbon dioxide.

steps: Identify the source: diesel oil is a fraction obtained from crude oil, a fossil fuel
Explain formation time: crude oil takes millions of years to form from the remains of dead sea organisms
Compare rates: we are using it much faster than it forms, so the supply is finite and will run out
worked.ans: Diesel oil comes from crude oil, which takes millions of years to form and is being used up much faster than it is made, so it will run out.

worked.q: A country has 2.4 billion barrels of oil reserves and uses 120 million barrels per year. Assuming use stays the same, estimate how many years the reserves will last, and give one reason why the real answer may differ.
steps: Convert to the same units: 2.4 billion = 2400 million barrels
Years = 2400 / 120 = 20 years
Reason it may differ: demand may increase (population growth) so reserves run out sooner
Or: new reserves may be discovered or extraction technology improve, so they last longer
Or: switching to renewables reduces use, so they last longer
worked.ans: About 20 years, but the real figure will differ because the rate of use and the known reserves both change over time.

worked.q: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced when 8.0 g of methane burns completely. (Ar: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
steps: Equation: CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O, so 1 mol CH4 gives 1 mol CO2
Mr of CH4 = 12 + 4 = 16, so moles = 8.0 / 16 = 0.50 mol
Moles of CO2 = 0.50 mol
Mass of CO2 = 0.50 × 44 = 22 g
worked.ans: 22 g of carbon dioxide, showing that burning fossil fuels releases a large mass of greenhouse gas.

chem_edx.8.7.summary: Crude oil contains far more long-chain hydrocarbons than people need, and far fewer of the short-chain ones that make good fuels such as petrol. **Cracking** fixes this mismatch: long-chain alkanes are heated and passed over a hot **catalyst of silica or alumina (about 600-700 °C)** so they break down into **shorter-chain alkanes** and **alkenes**. The shorter alkanes are used as fuels, and the alkenes are valuable starting materials for making polymers and other chemicals.

core.p: Cracking is a **thermal decomposition** reaction: heat breaks a large molecule into smaller ones. A **long-chain alkane** is split into a **shorter-chain alkane** and at least one **alkene**. Covalent C-C bonds in the chain break, and the products are smaller, more useful molecules.
bullets: Reactant: a long-chain alkane (saturated, general formula CnH2n+2), usually from a heavy fraction such as fuel oil or gas oil
Products: a shorter-chain alkane (saturated) AND an alkene (unsaturated, general formula CnH2n)
It is a decomposition: one reactant gives two or more products
No oxygen is involved, so it is NOT combustion
Atoms are conserved: the total number of C and H atoms is the same on both sides

callouts.p: The breaking down of long-chain alkanes into shorter-chain alkanes and alkenes, using heat and a catalyst.
An alkane can never crack into only alkanes: there are not enough hydrogen atoms. At least one product must be an alkene.

core.p: In industry the long-chain alkane is **vaporised** and passed over a **hot catalyst of silica (silicon dioxide) or alumina (aluminium oxide)** at about **600-700 °C**. The high temperature supplies the energy needed to break strong C-C bonds; the catalyst lowers the activation energy so cracking happens quickly at a lower temperature than without it.
bullets: Temperature: about **600-700 °C**
Catalyst: **silica** (SiO2) or **alumina** (Al2O3)
The alkane must be a vapour (gas) to pass over the catalyst
The catalyst is not used up, so it can be reused
Products are separated afterwards by fractional distillation

head: Condition

callouts.p: Edexcel mark schemes reward 'silica or alumina catalyst' AND 'high temperature (600-700 °C)'. Give both for full marks.

core.p: In the lab, **liquid paraffin** (a mixture of long-chain alkanes) is soaked into **mineral wool** at the end of a boiling tube. Pieces of **aluminium oxide** or broken porous pot act as the catalyst. The catalyst is heated strongly, and the paraffin is then warmed so its vapour passes over the hot catalyst. The gaseous products are collected over water.
bullets: Heat the catalyst first, then flick the flame to the mineral wool to vaporise the paraffin
Short-chain alkenes such as ethene are gases at room temperature, so they bubble into the collecting tube
Discard the first tube of gas: it is mostly air pushed out of the apparatus
Before stopping heating, **lift the delivery tube out of the water** to stop suck-back
Suck-back: as the hot tube cools, gas contracts and cold water is drawn back, which can crack the hot glass

callouts.p: Never stop heating while the delivery tube is still under the water. Remove the tube from the water first.

core.p: The two types of product are different families. **Alkanes are saturated**: every carbon atom has only single bonds. **Alkenes are unsaturated**: they contain a **carbon-carbon double bond (C=C)**. The double bond makes alkenes much **more reactive** than alkanes, which is exactly why they are useful to the chemical industry.
bullets: Alkanes: general formula CnH2n+2, e.g. methane CH4, ethane C2H6, propane C3H8
Alkenes: general formula CnH2n, e.g. ethene C2H4, propene C3H6, butene C4H8
Alkenes can join together to make **polymers** (e.g. ethene → poly(ethene))
Test for an alkene: shake with **bromine water**: orange to colourless
Alkanes leave bromine water orange (no reaction)

callouts.p: A hydrocarbon that contains at least one carbon-carbon double bond.

core.h: Why cracking is needed: supply and demand
core.p: Fractional distillation of crude oil produces **more long-chain hydrocarbons than are needed** (e.g. fuel oil, heavy gas oil) and **fewer short-chain hydrocarbons than are needed** (e.g. petrol). Supply of short chains is less than demand. Cracking converts the surplus heavy fractions into the products people actually want, so less crude oil is wasted.
bullets: **Supply** = how much of each fraction crude oil naturally contains
**Demand** = how much of each fraction people want to buy
Long-chain fractions: supply > demand (surplus)
Short-chain fractions such as petrol: demand > supply (shortage)
Cracking matches supply to demand and makes better use of a **finite resource**
It makes refining more profitable: low-value heavy fractions become high-value petrol and alkenes

callouts.p: Cracking is needed because (1) short-chain hydrocarbons are in higher demand than the supply from crude oil, and (2) it produces alkenes, which are used to make polymers.

core.h: Why short-chain hydrocarbons are more useful as fuels
core.p: Short-chain hydrocarbons make better fuels because of the trends in properties across the fractions. Shorter molecules have **weaker intermolecular forces**, so they are more **volatile**, **less viscous**, **easier to ignite** and burn with a **cleaner flame**.
bullets: Lower boiling point: vaporise easily, which a car engine needs
Higher volatility: evaporate readily to mix with air
Lower viscosity: flow easily through fuel pipes
More flammable: ignite easily
Burn more cleanly: less smoky, less soot
Long chains are thick, hard to ignite and smoky, so are less useful as fuels

callouts.p: Boiling hydrocarbons breaks the weak forces BETWEEN molecules, not the covalent bonds inside them. Cracking is different: it DOES break covalent C-C bonds.

core.p: Crude oil contains almost **no alkenes**, so cracking is the main source of them. Because the C=C double bond is reactive, alkenes are the **feedstock** (starting material) for the petrochemical industry.
bullets: Ethene → poly(ethene), used for plastic bags and bottles
Propene → poly(propene), used for crates and ropes
Alkenes are also used to make other chemicals, such as ethanol (from ethene and steam)
Without cracking there would be far too few alkenes for the plastics industry

callouts.p: Alkenes from cracking are a feedstock for making polymers. 'Polymers' or 'plastics' is the word mark schemes look for.

core.p: Cracking is **endothermic**: energy must be supplied continuously to break the C-C bonds. That is why a high temperature is needed. The catalyst does not provide energy; it gives an alternative pathway with a **lower activation energy**, so the reaction is faster and can run at a lower temperature, saving energy and money.
bullets: Thermal = by heating
Decomposition = breaking one substance into simpler substances
The bond broken is a covalent C-C bond in the hydrocarbon chain
Catalyst is unchanged at the end and can be reused

callouts.p: Cracking happens without oxygen. If you write that the alkane 'burns' or 'reacts with oxygen' you lose the mark.

core.p: Chains break at random positions, so cracking any single alkane gives a **mixture** of shorter alkanes and different alkenes, sometimes hydrogen as well. The mixture is then separated by **fractional distillation** into useful fractions.
bullets: The same alkane can give different products: C10H22 → C8H18 + C2H4 or C10H22 → C7H16 + C3H6
Conditions can be adjusted to favour the products that are most in demand
Refineries run cracking units alongside fractional distillation columns

core.h: Link to crude oil as a finite resource
core.p: Crude oil is **finite** (non-renewable): it formed over millions of years and is being used up far faster than it forms. Cracking allows **more of each barrel** to be turned into high-demand products, so less is wasted. It does not create new crude oil, and burning the petrol made still releases carbon dioxide.
bullets: Cracking improves the efficiency of using crude oil
It reduces the amount of heavy fractions with no buyers
It does not make crude oil renewable

callouts.p: In 6-mark answers, mention both the benefit (more petrol, alkenes for plastics, less waste) and that it needs a lot of energy to reach 600-700 °C.

core.h: Exam skills: interpreting supply and demand data
core.p: Edexcel often gives a table or bar chart of supply and demand for each fraction. Identify which fractions have **demand greater than supply** (these must be made by cracking) and which have **supply greater than demand** (these are cracked).
bullets: Compare the two numbers for each fraction and quote them in your answer
Fraction with surplus = suitable for cracking (long chains)
Fraction with shortage = product of cracking (short chains)
Use comparative words: 'supply is lower than demand'

callouts.p: 'Petrol: demand 24%, supply only 10%' scores more than 'petrol is in demand'.

analogy.p: A bakery bakes lots of very long baguettes (long-chain alkanes) but customers mostly want short rolls (petrol-sized molecules). Slicing the baguettes into rolls is like cracking, and the knife is like the catalyst: it makes the job much easier. The analogy breaks down because a cut baguette just gives shorter pieces of the same bread, whereas cracking gives two different kinds of product: a shorter alkane and an alkene with a double bond, because there are not enough hydrogen atoms to go round.

terms.d: Breaking down long-chain alkanes into shorter-chain alkanes and alkenes using heat and a catalyst.
A reaction in which heat breaks a substance down into two or more simpler substances.
A substance that speeds up a reaction by providing a pathway with lower activation energy, without being used up.
Silicon dioxide, SiO2; one catalyst used in cracking.
Aluminium oxide, Al2O3; a catalyst used in cracking.
A saturated hydrocarbon with only C-C single bonds; general formula CnH2n+2.
An unsaturated hydrocarbon containing a C=C double bond; general formula CnH2n.
Containing only single carbon-carbon bonds.
Containing at least one carbon-carbon double bond.
The amount of a fraction produced from crude oil by fractional distillation.
The amount of a fraction that people want to use.
A raw material used to make other chemicals, e.g. alkenes for polymers.
A very long molecule made by joining many small monomer molecules, e.g. poly(ethene) from ethene.
How easily a liquid evaporates; short-chain hydrocarbons are more volatile.
How thick a liquid is, or how slowly it flows; long chains are more viscous.
Water being drawn back into hot apparatus as gas inside cools and contracts.

mistakes.w: Cracking turns long alkanes into short alkanes.
mistakes.r: Cracking produces shorter-chain alkanes AND alkenes.

mistakes.w: Cracking is needed because long chains are useless.
mistakes.r: Supply of long-chain fractions is greater than demand, and demand for short-chain fractions is greater than supply.

mistakes.w: Cracking needs a high temperature and pressure.
mistakes.r: High temperature (600-700 °C) and a silica or alumina catalyst.

mistakes.w: The alkane burns / reacts with oxygen.
mistakes.r: It is thermal decomposition; no oxygen is involved.

mistakes.w: Alkenes are used as fuels.
mistakes.r: Alkenes are used to make polymers (plastics) and other chemicals; shorter alkanes are used as fuels.
Not balanced for hydrogen (22 vs 24); one product must be an alkene, e.g. C5H12 + C5H10.

mistakes.w: Cracking breaks intermolecular forces.
mistakes.r: Cracking breaks covalent C-C bonds within the molecule.

mistakes.w: The catalyst is iron.
mistakes.r: Silica or alumina (aluminium oxide); iron is the Haber process catalyst.

mistakes.w: Stop heating, then take the tube out of the water.
mistakes.r: Remove the delivery tube from the water before stopping heating, to prevent suck-back.

exam.q: State what is meant by cracking.
model: Breaking down long-chain alkanes into shorter-chain alkanes and alkenes
exam.tip: Name both products for the mark.

exam.q: Give the conditions used for cracking.
model: Temperature of about 600-700 °C
Silica or alumina catalyst
exam.tip: One mark each; 'heat' alone is too vague.

exam.q: Complete the equation: C12H26 → C8H18 + ____
model: C4H8
exam.tip: Subtract atom by atom: C 12-8=4, H 26-18=8.

exam.q: Decane, C10H22, is cracked to give ethene and one other product. Write a balanced equation.
model: Correct formulae and balanced
exam.tip: Check C and H totals on both sides.

exam.q: Explain why cracking is necessary.
model: Demand for short-chain hydrocarbons (e.g. petrol) is greater than supply from crude oil
Long-chain fractions are in surplus / cracking converts them into more useful products, including alkenes for polymers
exam.tip: Use the words supply and demand.

exam.q: State one use of the alkenes made by cracking.
model: Making polymers / plastics (e.g. poly(ethene))
exam.tip: 'Fuel' scores zero here.

exam.q: Describe a chemical test to show that a cracking product is an alkene.
model: Add bromine water and shake
Turns from orange to colourless
exam.tip: Say 'colourless', not 'clear'.

exam.q: Explain why short-chain hydrocarbons are more useful as fuels than long-chain hydrocarbons.
model: Lower boiling point / more volatile, so vaporise easily
Lower viscosity, so flow easily
More flammable / ignite easily
Burn with a cleaner, less smoky flame
exam.tip: Four distinct properties for four marks.

exam.q: In a lab cracking experiment, explain why the delivery tube must be removed from the water before heating is stopped.
model: As the tube cools the gas inside contracts / pressure falls
Cold water would be sucked back into the hot tube and crack the glass
exam.tip: Name 'suck-back' and explain the cause.

exam.q: The table shows supply and demand for fractions. Petrol: supply 10%, demand 24%. Fuel oil: supply 38%, demand 20%. Use the data to explain how cracking helps the refinery.
model: Demand for petrol (24%) is greater than supply (10%)
Supply of fuel oil (38%) is greater than demand (20%)
Fuel oil is cracked to make shorter-chain hydrocarbons such as petrol
So supply better matches demand / less waste and more profit; alkenes also produced for polymers
exam.tip: Quote numbers from the data.

exam.q: Describe how long-chain alkanes are converted into more useful products and explain why this process is carried out. (6 marks)
model: Long-chain alkanes are vaporised / heated
Passed over a hot catalyst of silica or alumina
At about 600-700 °C
Thermal decomposition breaks C-C bonds giving shorter alkanes and alkenes, e.g. C10H22 → C8H18 + C2H4
Demand for short-chain fractions such as petrol exceeds supply; long-chain fractions are in surplus
Shorter alkanes are used as fuels and alkenes are used to make polymers
exam.tip: Cover both 'how' and 'why'; an equation is a quick way to show products.

worked.q: Hexadecane, C16H34, is cracked to produce octane, C8H18, and ethene only. How many ethene molecules form per hexadecane molecule? Write the equation.
steps: Carbon left over: 16 - 8 = 8 carbon atoms
Hydrogen left over: 34 - 18 = 16 hydrogen atoms
Leftover is C8H16; ethene is C2H4
8 ÷ 2 = 4 and 16 ÷ 4 = 4, so 4 ethene molecules

worked.q: A student says C10H22 → C6H14 + C4H10. Explain why this is wrong and correct it.
steps: Count hydrogen: left 22, right 14 + 10 = 24
Hydrogen does not balance; two alkanes need more hydrogen than one alkane has
One product must be an alkene with formula CnH2n
Keep C6H14 (alkane); the other product must be C4H8 (butene)
worked.ans: C10H22 → C6H14 + C4H8; the products must include an alkene.

worked.q: Model answer: explain why oil companies crack the fuel oil fraction.
steps: Fuel oil contains long-chain hydrocarbons and crude oil supplies more of it than is needed
Petrol contains short-chain hydrocarbons and demand is greater than supply
Cracking fuel oil at 600-700 °C over silica or alumina makes shorter alkanes for petrol
It also makes alkenes, which are a feedstock for polymers
So less crude oil is wasted and the refinery earns more
worked.ans: Cracking converts surplus low-demand long chains into high-demand petrol and alkenes, matching supply to demand.

chem_edx.8.8.summary: Scientists think Earth's **early atmosphere** came from gases released by **volcanoes**: mainly **carbon dioxide** and **water vapour**, with **little or no oxygen**. As the Earth cooled, the water vapour **condensed** to form the **oceans**, and carbon dioxide then **dissolved** in them, was locked into **carbonate sedimentary rocks** and later into fossil fuels. When primitive plants and algae began to **photosynthesise**, they removed more carbon dioxide and released **oxygen**, which slowly built up to the 21% we have today.

core.p: The early atmosphere formed about **4.6 billion years ago**, long before anyone could measure it. Scientists therefore **interpret indirect evidence** and build models. Because the evidence is limited and indirect, theories about the early atmosphere have **changed over time** and are still debated.
bullets: No direct samples: the oldest air trapped in ice is less than about one million years old
Evidence from the gases released by **volcanoes today**
Evidence from **rocks**: the types of rock and minerals that formed at different times
Evidence from the atmospheres of other planets such as **Mars and Venus**, which are mostly carbon dioxide
Fossils show when living organisms such as algae appeared

callouts.p: Edexcel asks you to 'interpret evidence'. Always link a piece of evidence to the conclusion it supports, e.g. 'modern volcanoes release mostly CO2 and water vapour, so the early atmosphere probably did too'.

core.h: Volcanic origin of the early atmosphere
core.p: The young Earth was extremely hot and had intense **volcanic activity**. The volcanoes released gases that formed the early atmosphere. Most scientists think it was **mainly carbon dioxide** with **water vapour**, and **little or no oxygen**, plus smaller amounts of other gases such as nitrogen, methane and ammonia.
bullets: Carbon dioxide: the main gas
Water vapour: large amounts, later condensed into oceans
Little or no oxygen
Some nitrogen and small amounts of methane and ammonia
Similar to the atmospheres of Mars and Venus today

callouts.p: Mostly carbon dioxide and water vapour from volcanoes, with little or no oxygen.

core.p: As the Earth **cooled**, its surface temperature fell below 100 °C. The **water vapour condensed** into liquid water, which fell as rain and collected in low-lying areas to form the **oceans**. This removed most of the water vapour from the atmosphere.
bullets: Cooling caused condensation: water vapour (gas) → liquid water
Rain over a very long time filled the oceans
The oceans then gave carbon dioxide somewhere to dissolve
Liquid water was also essential for the first living organisms

callouts.p: The change of state from gas to liquid when a substance is cooled.

core.h: How carbon dioxide was reduced: dissolving in the oceans
core.p: Once the oceans formed, a large amount of **carbon dioxide dissolved** in the water. The dissolved carbon dioxide reacted to form **carbonate compounds**, which **precipitated** out and settled on the sea bed.
bullets: Carbon dioxide is fairly soluble in water
Dissolved CO2 formed carbonates such as calcium carbonate
Carbonates settled as sediments on the sea floor
This removed carbon dioxide from the atmosphere

core.h: Carbon locked up in sedimentary rocks
core.p: Over millions of years, layers of carbonate sediment and the **shells and skeletons of marine organisms** (made of calcium carbonate) were compressed to form **sedimentary rocks** such as **limestone**. The carbon in these rocks was taken out of the atmosphere for a very long time.
bullets: Marine organisms used dissolved carbonate to build shells
When they died, shells sank and built up on the sea bed
Compression over millions of years formed limestone and chalk
Limestone is mainly calcium carbonate, CaCO3

callouts.p: Carbonate sedimentary rocks like limestone are a huge store of carbon removed from the early atmosphere.

core.h: Fossil fuels as another carbon store
core.p: Carbon taken in by plants, algae and marine organisms was also trapped when their remains were buried. Over millions of years, heat and pressure turned the remains into **fossil fuels**: **coal** (from plants) and **crude oil and natural gas** (from marine plankton). This locked more carbon away from the atmosphere.
bullets: Coal formed from the remains of land plants
Crude oil and natural gas formed from tiny sea organisms (plankton)
Burning fossil fuels today returns this stored carbon to the air as carbon dioxide

core.p: Primitive **plants and algae** (and photosynthetic bacteria) appeared, probably around **2.7 billion years ago**. They used carbon dioxide for **photosynthesis**, which further **decreased the carbon dioxide** in the atmosphere. The carbon became part of their cells.
bullets: Word equation: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen
Symbol equation: 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2
Needs energy from light, absorbed by chlorophyll
Every 6 molecules of CO2 removed release 6 molecules of O2

callouts.p: Photosynthesis both removes carbon dioxide AND releases oxygen into the atmosphere.

core.p: Before life, there was little or no oxygen. **Oxygen gradually increased** because of **photosynthesis** by algae and later green plants. At first the oxygen reacted with iron and other substances in rocks and the oceans, so it took hundreds of millions of years for oxygen to build up in the air. Eventually it reached about **21%**, enough for animals to evolve.
bullets: Source of oxygen: photosynthesis by algae and plants
Early oxygen was used up oxidising iron in rocks, forming iron oxides
Rocks containing iron oxide that formed only after a certain time are evidence oxygen was appearing
Oxygen also formed the ozone layer, which absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation, allowing life on land
More oxygen allowed more complex organisms to evolve

callouts.p: Oxygen did NOT come from volcanoes. It came from photosynthesis.

core.p: Nitrogen is very **unreactive**, so once in the atmosphere it was not removed by reactions and it gradually **accumulated** until it became the main gas. Today's dry air is roughly **78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.9% argon and 0.04% carbon dioxide**, with small amounts of other gases.
bullets: Nitrogen: about 78%
Oxygen: about 21%
Argon: about 0.9% (a noble gas)
Carbon dioxide: about 0.04%
Water vapour varies and is usually left out of 'dry air' figures

core.p: Putting the steps in order is a common exam task. The changes happened over **billions of years**.
bullets: About 4.6 billion years ago: Earth forms; intense volcanic activity releases CO2 and water vapour
Earth cools: water vapour condenses to form oceans
CO2 dissolves in the oceans; carbonates form and become sedimentary rocks
About 2.7 billion years ago: algae and plants start photosynthesising, removing CO2 and releasing O2
Oxygen slowly builds up; carbon is locked in fossil fuels and rocks
Today: about 78% N2, 21% O2, 0.9% Ar, 0.04% CO2

callouts.p: Use 'first', 'then', 'as the Earth cooled', 'later' to show the order clearly in 6-mark answers.

core.p: The big changes are: **carbon dioxide went from the main gas to a tiny percentage**, **oxygen went from almost none to about a fifth**, and **water vapour fell** because it formed the oceans. Questions often ask you to describe a change and explain its cause.
bullets: CO2 decreased: dissolved in oceans, locked into carbonate rocks and fossil fuels, used in photosynthesis
O2 increased: produced by photosynthesis
Water vapour decreased: condensed to form oceans
N2 increased in proportion: unreactive so it built up

head: Change
Cause
rows: Condensed as Earth cooled, forming oceans
Dissolved in oceans; formed sedimentary rocks; photosynthesis; fossil fuels

core.p: Each piece of evidence supports part of the theory, but none is complete. Good answers say what the evidence shows and why it is not certain.
bullets: Modern volcanoes release mainly CO2 and water vapour: supports a volcanic origin
Mars and Venus have CO2-rich atmospheres: suggests young rocky planets had CO2 atmospheres
Large limestone deposits: show huge amounts of CO2 were removed
Fossil algae and iron oxide rock layers: show when oxygen started to appear
Limitation: events happened billions of years ago with no direct measurements, so conclusions are based on models and may change

callouts.p: Say 'scientists think' or 'evidence suggests', not 'it is proven'. Mark schemes reward recognising uncertainty.

analogy.p: Imagine a bath full of fizzy cola (carbon dioxide). Over time you pour most of it away into bottles you seal and store in the cellar (rocks and fossil fuels), and a tap slowly drips in fresh water (oxygen from photosynthesis) until the bath is mostly a different liquid. The analogy works because CO2 was not destroyed but stored, and oxygen was added gradually. It breaks down because the 'storage' happened by chemical reactions and living things over billions of years, and most of today's air is nitrogen, which in the analogy has no matching ingredient.

terms.d: Earth's atmosphere about 4 billion years ago, mainly carbon dioxide and water vapour with little or no oxygen.
Eruptions that release gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapour from inside the Earth.
Change of state from gas to liquid on cooling.
Water vapour condensing as the Earth cooled and falling as rain to collect as oceans.
When a substance mixes into a liquid to form a solution, e.g. CO2 in sea water.
A compound containing the carbonate ion, CO3 2-, such as calcium carbonate.
An insoluble solid formed from a solution.
Rock formed from layers of sediment compressed over millions of years, e.g. limestone.
A sedimentary rock made mainly of calcium carbonate, CaCO3, often from shells of marine organisms.
Process in plants and algae: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, using light energy.
Simple photosynthesising organisms, among the first to release oxygen into the atmosphere.
Coal, crude oil or natural gas, formed from the remains of ancient organisms over millions of years.
Something that locks carbon away from the atmosphere, such as oceans, rocks and fossil fuels.
A layer of ozone (O3) high in the atmosphere, formed from oxygen, that absorbs ultraviolet radiation.
Unreactive gas that makes up about 78% of today's atmosphere.
Observations or data used to support or test a scientific theory.

Water vapour
exam.tip: 'Steam' is accepted for water vapour, but 'water' alone may not be.

exam.q: State where the gases of the early atmosphere came from.

exam.tip: One word answer is fine.

exam.q: Explain how the oceans formed.
model: The Earth cooled
Water vapour condensed (to liquid water / rain) and collected to form oceans
exam.tip: Use the word 'condensed'.

exam.q: Explain how the amount of oxygen in the atmosphere increased.
model: Algae / plants evolved
Photosynthesis released oxygen
exam.tip: Name photosynthesis explicitly.

exam.q: Write the balanced symbol equation for photosynthesis.
model: Correct formulae (1), balancing (1)
exam.tip: Glucose is C6H12O6.

exam.q: Give two ways in which carbon dioxide was removed from the early atmosphere.
model: Dissolved in the oceans (forming carbonates / sedimentary rocks)
Used in photosynthesis by plants and algae / locked in fossil fuels
exam.tip: Two different processes for two marks.

exam.q: Explain why scientists cannot be certain about the composition of the early atmosphere.
model: It was billions of years ago / no one was there to measure it
Evidence is limited / indirect, so conclusions are based on interpretation
exam.tip: Mention both time and limited evidence.

exam.q: Modern volcanoes release mainly carbon dioxide and water vapour. Explain how this is used as evidence about the early atmosphere.
model: Early Earth had lots of volcanic activity
If early volcanoes released similar gases, the early atmosphere would have been mostly CO2 and water vapour
exam.tip: Link the evidence to the conclusion.

exam.q: Describe how carbon dioxide from the early atmosphere ended up in limestone.
model: Carbon dioxide dissolved in the oceans
Formed carbonates / used by marine organisms to make shells (calcium carbonate)
These settled and were compressed over millions of years into sedimentary rock (limestone)
exam.tip: Give the steps in order.

exam.q: Compare Earth's early atmosphere with today's atmosphere.
model: Early: mostly carbon dioxide; today only about 0.04%
Early: little or no oxygen; today about 21%
Early: lots of water vapour; today very little (formed oceans)
Today mostly nitrogen, about 78%
exam.tip: Each point should say early AND today.

exam.q: Describe and explain how Earth's atmosphere has changed from its early composition to today's composition. (6 marks)
model: Early atmosphere from volcanoes: mainly CO2 and water vapour, little or no oxygen
Earth cooled and water vapour condensed to form oceans
CO2 dissolved in oceans and formed carbonate precipitates
Carbonates / shells formed sedimentary rocks such as limestone
Algae and plants photosynthesised: 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2, removing CO2 and releasing O2
Some carbon locked in fossil fuels; oxygen built up to about 21%; nitrogen unreactive so it built up to about 78%
exam.tip: Cover water, carbon dioxide and oxygen in a logical order.

worked.q: Model answer (4 marks): Explain why the percentage of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere decreased.
steps: As the Earth cooled, oceans formed and carbon dioxide dissolved in them
Dissolved carbon dioxide formed carbonates that precipitated, and marine organisms used it to make calcium carbonate shells
These were compressed into sedimentary rocks such as limestone, locking the carbon away
Algae and plants used carbon dioxide in photosynthesis; their buried remains formed fossil fuels
worked.ans: CO2 decreased by dissolving in oceans, forming carbonate rocks, photosynthesis and being trapped in fossil fuels.

worked.q: Applied example: photosynthesis uses 6 molecules of CO2 to release how many molecules of O2? What does this show about the early atmosphere?
steps: Equation: 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2
6 molecules of CO2 removed for every 6 molecules of O2 released, a 1 : 1 ratio
So as photosynthesis spread, CO2 fell while O2 rose
worked.ans: 6 molecules of O2; photosynthesis explains both the fall in CO2 and the rise in O2.

worked.q: A student says, 'Mars has an atmosphere of about 95% carbon dioxide, so Earth's early atmosphere was definitely 95% carbon dioxide.' Evaluate this statement.
steps: Supports: Mars is a rocky planet with volcanic history, so its atmosphere suggests young rocky planets had CO2-rich atmospheres
Against: Mars is a different size and temperature and has no life or oceans, so conditions differed
The evidence is indirect, so the exact percentage cannot be known
Conclusion: it supports the idea that the early atmosphere was mainly CO2, but 'definitely 95%' is not justified
worked.ans: The evidence supports a CO2-rich early atmosphere, but the exact figure is uncertain, so 'definitely' is wrong.

chem_edx.8.9.summary: The test for oxygen is simple: put a **glowing splint** into a test tube of the gas, and if the gas is oxygen the **splint relights**. This works because oxygen **supports combustion**: air contains only about 21% oxygen, so a glowing splint just smoulders in air, but in pure or concentrated oxygen the burning reaction speeds up enough to burst back into flame. You need to know the method, the exact result, why it happens, and how it differs from the tests for hydrogen, carbon dioxide and chlorine.

core.p: To test for oxygen, light a wooden splint, **blow it out so it is just glowing**, and quickly put it into the mouth of a test tube of the gas. If oxygen is present, the **glowing splint relights** (bursts back into flame).
bullets: Test: insert a **glowing splint** into the gas
Positive result: the splint **relights**
Negative result: the splint stays glowing or goes out
Do the test quickly so the gas does not escape or mix with air
Keep the test tube upright or stoppered until testing; oxygen is slightly denser than air

callouts.p: A glowing splint relights in oxygen.
A LIT splint is the test for hydrogen (squeaky pop). For oxygen the splint must be GLOWING and the result is that it RELIGHTS.

core.p: A precise method is often worth marks. Each step has a reason.
bullets: Collect the gas in a test tube and keep it stoppered (or upside down over water)
Light a wooden splint in a Bunsen flame
Blow the flame out so only the tip glows red
Remove the stopper and immediately put the glowing tip into the mouth of the tube
Observe: if the splint relights, the gas is oxygen
Do not push the splint into any liquid: water would put it out

callouts.p: Write 'the glowing splint relights'. 'Burns brighter', 'glows more' or 'ignites' may not get the mark.

core.p: Oxygen **supports combustion**: it is the reactant that a fuel needs to burn. The glowing tip is wood (mainly carbon compounds) reacting slowly with oxygen. In air there are fewer oxygen molecules, so the reaction is too slow to keep a flame. In pure oxygen there are many more oxygen molecules in the same volume, so there are **more frequent collisions**, the reaction rate increases, and enough heat is released for the wood to burst into flame.
bullets: Air is about 21% oxygen and 78% nitrogen; nitrogen does not support combustion
Pure oxygen has about five times the concentration of oxygen molecules as air
Higher concentration → more frequent successful collisions → faster reaction
Faster reaction releases heat faster, so the wood reaches ignition and flames again
Oxygen does not burn itself; it helps other substances burn

callouts.p: Oxygen supports combustion but is not flammable itself. Say 'oxygen supports combustion', not 'oxygen burns'.

core.p: The wood of the splint is a fuel containing carbon and hydrogen. When it burns in oxygen it undergoes **combustion**, an exothermic oxidation reaction.
bullets: Simplified: carbon + oxygen → carbon dioxide
C + O2 → CO2
Hydrogen in the wood forms water: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O (simplified idea)
The reaction is exothermic: it gives out heat and light
The glowing tip shows a slow combustion; the flame shows fast combustion

core.p: Oxygen is usually made by **decomposing hydrogen peroxide** using **manganese(IV) oxide** (MnO2) as a **catalyst**. The hydrogen peroxide breaks down into water and oxygen; the catalyst speeds up the reaction and is not used up.
bullets: Word equation: hydrogen peroxide → water + oxygen
Symbol equation: 2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2
Manganese(IV) oxide is a black powder and is unchanged at the end
Bubbles of a colourless gas form
The gas can be collected over water, then tested with a glowing splint

callouts.p: 2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2: 4 H and 4 O on each side.

core.p: Oxygen is only **slightly soluble in water**, so it can be **collected over water**: bubbles push water out of an upturned, water-filled test tube. It can also be collected in a gas syringe to measure its volume. Because oxygen is slightly denser than air, a stoppered tube held upright keeps it for a short time.
bullets: Over water: simple and lets you see when the tube is full
Gas syringe: measures volume, useful for rate experiments
Discard the first tube: it is mostly air displaced from the apparatus
Stopper the tube under water before lifting it out

core.p: Edexcel expects you to know the tests for **hydrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide and chlorine**. Exam questions often mix them up, so learn each test and result as a pair.
bullets: Oxygen: glowing splint **relights**
Hydrogen: lighted splint gives a **squeaky pop** (hydrogen burns: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O)
Carbon dioxide: bubble through **limewater**, which turns **milky (cloudy)**
Chlorine: **damp blue litmus paper** turns red then is **bleached white**

callouts.p: Glowing splint relights = OXYGEN. Lighted splint squeaky pop = HYDROGEN. Never put a lit splint in the oxygen answer.
